Here, we present a combined single crystal neutron diffraction, X-ray resonant magnetic scattering, and single crystal X-ray diffraction study of TbCuAs$_2$. These measurements unambiguously determine the Tb magnetic moment direction, the antiferromagnetic arrangement along high symmetry directions, the interplay between structure and magnetism, and their temperature dependence. Our observations are compared with previous studies on sister compounds in the rare-earth copper arsenide family ($R$CuAs$_2$, $R$ = Sm and Gd), which also displays resistivity anomalies. We suggest a common underlying physics governing the structural and magentic properties of rare-earth copper arsenides that exhibit low-temperature resistivity anomalies.

AI.tldr: A combined neutron diffraction, X-ray resonant magnetic scattering, and single-crystal X-ray diffraction study of TbCuAs2 unambiguously determines the Tb magnetic moment direction, the antiferromagnetic arrangement, and the structure-magnetism interplay, suggesting a common underlying physics across rare-earth copper arsenides with low-temperature resistivity anomalies.
AI.motivation: TbCuAs2 is an antiferromagnetic metal showing an anomalous low-temperature resistivity upturn, proposed to arise from its magnetic ground state. However, the precise nature of its antiferromagnetic ordering had not been previously established, motivating a detailed determination of its magnetic and structural properties.
AI.method: The authors performed a combined experimental study using single-crystal neutron diffraction, X-ray resonant magnetic scattering, and single-crystal X-ray diffraction on TbCuAs2 to resolve the magnetic moment direction, antiferromagnetic arrangement along high-symmetry directions, structure-magnetism interplay, and their temperature dependence.
AI.result: The measurements unambiguously determined the Tb magnetic moment direction, the antiferromagnetic arrangement along high-symmetry directions, the interplay between structure and magnetism, and their temperature dependence. Observations were compared with previous studies on sister compounds RCuAs2 (R = Sm, Gd), which also exhibit resistivity anomalies.
AI.conclusion: The authors suggest a common underlying physics governing the structural and magnetic properties of rare-earth copper arsenides that exhibit low-temperature resistivity anomalies.

title: NTBuilder: Commensurate Construction of Nanotubes from Arbitrary Two-Dimensional Crystals and a Catalog of 20 Million Structures
summary: Although tens of thousands of two-dimensional (2D) crystals are now known, the nanotubes they can form are usually constructed for individual materials, using procedures derived for graphene. Here, we develop a general theory of the rolling construction for arbitrary 2D crystals and implement it in \ntbuilder{} (NanoTube Builder), an open-source library with desktop and web interfaces. We express the size of the exact unit cell of a tube through the reduced form of a single rational number built from the lattice metric, which explains why triangular and square lattices always close with small cells, whereas rectangular, centered rectangular, and oblique lattices can require cells larger by many orders of magnitude. The optimal approximate cells are the best rational approximations of a second number, so that a cell small enough for first-principles calculations can be chosen with a controlled departure from periodicity, as in the biphenylene network, where such a cell is eight orders of magnitude smaller than the exact one. The 17 plane groups reduce to seven distinct chirality maps once rolling is taken into account, the rolling sense of layers without a horizontal mirror defines distinct tubes, and bonds formed or broken by curvature are detected pair by pair against the flat layer. The same framework assembles multiwalled tubes whose walls share one axial period, periodic bundles, and strained or twisted structures that remain periodic. Applied to 46,403 distinct 2D systems, it produced a public catalog of 20,334,372 nanotubes, of which 57.1\% show no bond change upon rolling. All structures can be exported directly as input for first-principles and molecular dynamics codes.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a general theory for rolling arbitrary 2D crystals into nanotubes and implement it as open-source software (ntbuilder), yielding a catalog of over 20 million nanotubes.
AI.motivation: Existing nanotube construction methods are tailored to individual materials and largely derived from graphene procedures, so there is no general framework applicable to arbitrary 2D crystals.
AI.method: They formulate a general rolling theory for arbitrary 2D crystals, expressing the exact unit cell size of a tube via the reduced form of a rational number derived from the lattice metric. Optimal approximate cells are obtained as best rational approximations of a second number. The framework uses the 17 plane groups reduced to seven chirality maps, distinguishes rolling senses for layers lacking a horizontal mirror, detects curvature-formed/broken bonds pairwise against the flat layer, and assembles multiwalled tubes, bundles, and strained/twisted periodic structures. Implemented in ntbuilder with desktop and web interfaces.
AI.result: Triangular and square lattices always close with small cells, whereas rectangular, centered rectangular, and oblique lattices can require cells larger by many orders of magnitude. Small approximate cells with controlled departure from periodicity (e.g., biphenylene network: eight orders of magnitude smaller than exact) enable first-principles calculations. Application to 46,403 distinct 2D systems produced a public catalog of 20,334,372 nanotubes, 57.1% showing no bond change upon rolling. All structures export directly as input for first-principles and molecular dynamics codes.
AI.conclusion: A unified, general theory and open-source tool enable systematic construction, analysis, and high-throughput cataloging of nanotubes from arbitrary 2D crystals, with direct export for computational studies.

title: Can Chemically Inspired Parameter Initialization Mitigate Barren Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers?
summary: Recent advances in the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) have strengthened its promise for molecular electronic-structure calculations on near-term noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. However, barren plateaus (BPs) remain a major obstacle to scaling VQE, as vanishing gradients can severely obstruct optimization at large scale. While most BP studies focus on randomly initialized circuits and global gradient behavior, practical quantum chemistry VQE typically uses chemically motivated initializations and local optimization around HF- or MP2-derived states. Although chemically informed initializations are widely expected to improve VQE trainability, how they mitigate local barren plateaus remains unclear. We therefore study the occurrence of local barren plateaus in molecular UCCSD-VQE, considering both chemically motivated initialization points and iterates along the corresponding optimization trajectories. In the benchmarks considered here, chemically initialized starting points and variational trajectories show polynomial decay of local gradient variance with system size instead of the exponential BP-like decay observed for random controls, indicating that chemical initialization mitigates barren plateaus in the local optimization regions and highlights the trainability advantage of chemically motivated VQE strategies.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether chemically motivated initializations (HF/MP2-derived) mitigate barren plateaus in UCCSD-VQE. Results show local gradient variance decays polynomially with system size for chemically initialized points and trajectories, unlike the exponential decay seen with random controls, indicating improved trainability in local optimization regions.
AI.motivation: Barren plateaus (BPs) impede scaling of VQE for molecular electronic-structure calculations on NISQ devices. Most BP studies focus on randomly initialized circuits and global gradients, whereas practical quantum chemistry VQE uses chemically motivated initializations with local optimization. It is unclear how such informed initializations mitigate local barren plateaus, which this work aims to clarify.
AI.method: The study examines the occurrence of local barren plateaus in molecular UCCSD-VQE, analyzing both chemically motivated initialization points and iterates along the corresponding optimization trajectories. Local gradient variance scaling with system size is compared against random controls.
AI.result: For the benchmarks considered, chemically initialized starting points and their variational trajectories exhibit polynomial decay of local gradient variance with system size, rather than the exponential BP-like decay observed for randomly initialized controls.
AI.conclusion: Chemical initialization mitigates barren plateaus within local optimization regions, highlighting the trainability advantage of chemically motivated VQE strategies over random initialization approaches.

title: A rank-two spherical transform for eigenvector and singular-vector overlaps
summary: We define a rank-two extension $\mathcal{H}^{(2)}$ of the spherical $\mathcal{H}$-transform, together with its associated transform $\mathcal{R}^{(2)}$. For sums, both transforms are additive. The transform $\mathcal{R}^{(2)}$ yields a $4\times4$ formula for the average product of two hermitized resolvents, and hence for off-diagonal eigenvector overlaps, recovering the Ginibre, elliptic, and bi-invariant formulas. We also treat correlated pairs of matrices, and obtain overlaps between their eigenvectors or singular vectors.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a rank-two extension of the spherical H-transform and its associated R-transform, providing a 4×4 formula for averaged products of two hermitized resolvents and eigenvector overlaps, unifying Ginibre, elliptic, and bi-invariant cases.
AI.motivation: Eigenvector overlaps and resolvent products are central objects in random matrix theory, but existing transforms (spherical H-transform) handle only rank-one or simpler settings. A systematic framework extending to rank-two is needed to capture off-diagonal eigenvector overlaps and correlated matrix pairs.
AI.method: The authors define a rank-two extension of the spherical H-transform, denoted H^(2), and its associated transform R^(2). Additivity for sums is established. The R^(2)-transform is used to derive a 4×4 formula for the average product of two hermitized resolvents, which is then applied to eigenvector overlaps, including correlated pairs of matrices.
AI.result: The R^(2)-transform yields a 4×4 formula for the average product of two hermitized resolvents, giving off-diagonal eigenvector overlaps. It recovers the Ginibre, elliptic, and bi-invariant formulas as special cases. For correlated pairs of matrices, overlaps between their eigenvectors or singular vectors are obtained.
AI.conclusion: The rank-two spherical H-transform framework provides a unified and systematic tool for computing eigenvector overlaps and resolvent products, generalizing known results and extending to correlated matrix pairs.

title: Exact ballistic energy transport and emergent XXZ dynamics in an integrable three-state chain
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures; exact symbolic verification code included as arXiv ancillary files
summary: We investigate the coupling dependence of ballistic energy transport and the emergent spin dynamics in an integrable Hermitian three-state chain that connects a clock interaction to a highly degenerate flag limit. By constructing a regular $R$-matrix to establish a globally conserved energy current, we analytically evaluate its full variance to obtain the exact, strictly positive leading high-temperature coefficient of the thermal Drude weight and the ballistic growth rate of the energy-correlation second moment. In the strong-coupling limit, the degeneracy is lifted by virtual transitions of a delocalized third-color spectator state, which generates an effective spin-$1/2$ XXZ Hamiltonian with anisotropy $Δ= -1/2$ and fundamentally selects the all-active two-color sector as the true ground state. For periodic boundaries, this virtual spectator motion introduces a positive length-changing XXZ supercharge squared that, for $L\ge4$, strictly annihilates all states within a finite, length-independent energy interval above the ground state. Consequently, we rigorously prove that the full periodic effective theory perfectly replicates the exact low-energy XXZ spectrum, including all state multiplicities, as well as its macroscopic bulk free-energy density.

AI.tldr: The paper studies ballistic energy transport and emergent spin dynamics in an integrable Hermitian three-state chain connecting a clock interaction to a highly degenerate flag limit, deriving an exact thermal Drude weight and an effective spin-1/2 XXZ description in the strong-coupling limit.
AI.motivation: Understanding how ballistic energy transport and spin dynamics emerge from an integrable multi-state chain, and how a highly degenerate flag limit is resolved by coupling, is the central motivation.
AI.method: The authors construct a regular R-matrix to establish a globally conserved energy current, analytically evaluate its full variance to get the exact leading high-temperature thermal Drude weight and the ballistic growth rate of the energy-correlation second moment. They then analyze the strong-coupling limit where virtual transitions of a delocalized third-color spectator state lift the degeneracy, producing an effective spin-1/2 XXZ Hamiltonian with anisotropy Δ = -1/2, and study its periodic-boundary supercharge and low-energy spectrum.
AI.result: They obtain an exact, strictly positive leading high-temperature coefficient of the thermal Drude weight and the ballistic growth rate. In the strong-coupling limit, the effective spin-1/2 XXZ Hamiltonian with Δ = -1/2 selects the all-active two-color sector as the true ground state. For periodic boundaries, the virtual spectator motion yields a positive length-changing XXZ supercharge squared that, for L ≥ 4, strictly annihilates all states in a finite, length-independent energy interval above the ground state. The full periodic effective theory rigorously replicates the exact low-energy XXZ spectrum, including all multiplicities, and its macroscopic bulk free-energy density.
AI.conclusion: The coupling-induced virtual spectator dynamics provides an exact mapping between the three-state chain and an effective XXZ theory, reproducing the low-energy spectrum and bulk thermodynamics, thereby establishing ballistic energy transport and emergent spin physics in this integrable model.

title: Understanding Ideality Factor in Wide-Band Gap Semiconductor Devices with Strong Recombination Planes
summary: Ideality factor of a diode will depend on the location of the plane of maximum recombination within the diode's depletion region. It will have a minimum of one, but can range up to infinity depending on placement of the plane. Case studies analyzed in this work demonstrate better agreement with experimental data from GaN-based p-i-n diodes.

AI.tldr: The diode ideality factor is determined by the position of the maximum-recombination plane within the depletion region; it saturates at a minimum of 1 but can grow arbitrarily large. This spatial framework reproduces experimental GaN p-i-n diode data better than conventional models.
AI.motivation: Standard treatments of the diode ideality factor assume it is close to unity and attribute deviations mainly to carrier transport mechanisms, neglecting where recombination physically peaks inside the depletion region. The paper is motivated by the need to explain the anomalously large ideality factors observed in GaN-based p-i-n diodes.
AI.method: The ideality factor is expressed as a function of the location of the plane of maximum recombination within the depletion region. Case studies are then analyzed by comparing the position-dependent predictions against measured characteristics of GaN-based p-i-n diodes.
AI.result: The formulation yields an ideality factor with a lower bound of 1 that can rise toward infinity as the maximum-recombination plane shifts. The case studies show improved agreement with experimental GaN p-i-n diode data relative to conventional constant-ideality-factor treatments.
AI.conclusion: Positioning the plane of maximum recombination provides a simple, physically grounded route to modeling ideality factors above unity, and it offers a better description of GaN p-i-n diode behavior than standard assumptions.

title: Bulk Superconductivity in Rocksalt LaN$_{1-x}$
summary: We report the synthesis and characterization of lanthanum nitride by direct reaction of lanthanum metal with high pressure nitrogen gas in a laser floating-zone furnace. Combined synchrotron X-ray and neutron diffraction measurement verifies a rocksalt structure with stoichiometry LaN$_{0.94}$, consistent with first principles prediction that LaN is dynamically unstable in the stoichiometric limit. Electrical transport, heat capacity, and magnetization measurements show that LaN$_{0.94}$ is metallic with a superconducting transition at $T_c=5.95$ K. Our data establish LaN as the first bulk superconducting member of the rare earth mononitride family and motivates future exploration of the series using the unique processing space afforded by high-pressure optical reactors.

AI.tldr: LaN is synthesized via direct reaction of La metal with high-pressure N₂ in a laser floating-zone furnace; it adopts a rocksalt structure with stoichiometry LaN₀.₉₄ (LaN being dynamically unstable at the stoichiometric limit) and is metallic with bulk superconductivity at T_c = 5.95 K, making it the first bulk superconducting rare earth mononitride.
AI.motivation: The rare earth mononitride family lacks a confirmed bulk superconducting member; high-pressure optical reactors offer an unexplored processing space to stabilize such nitrides and test first-principles predictions of their (in)stability.
AI.method: Direct reaction of lanthanum metal with high-pressure nitrogen gas in a laser floating-zone furnace; characterization by combined synchrotron X-ray and neutron diffraction (structure/stoichiometry), plus electrical transport, heat capacity, and magnetization measurements; comparison with first-principles predictions.
AI.result: A rocksalt structure with stoichiometry LaN₀.₉₄ was confirmed by diffraction, in agreement with the predicted dynamical instability of stoichiometric LaN. Transport, heat capacity, and magnetization data show metallic behavior with a superconducting transition at T_c = 5.95 K.
AI.conclusion: LaN is established as the first bulk superconducting member of the rare earth mononitride series, motivating further exploration of the family using high-pressure optical reactors.

title: Magnetic Quadrupole Lens and Current-Induced Quadrupolar Dynamics of Antiskyrmion
summary: We demonstrate that antiskyrmions can serve as magnetic quadrupole lenses that focus or defocus electric currents traversing them. We showcase the antiskyrmion core as a focal point where electron beams converge for specific injection directions, leading to anisotropic and nonuniform current distributions. Thus the current-induced antiskyrmion dynamics is profoundly modified by the magnetic quadrupole lensing via the spin-transfer torque. By incorporating quantum transport and micromagnetic simulations iteratively, we self-consistently capture the coupled dynamics of conduction electrons and antiskyrmions. Our results unveil a quadrupolar antiskyrmion Hall effect that is highly anisotropic with respect to the current direction and can be effectively tuned by the spin-orbit coupling. In particular, the current focusing (defocusing) dramatically enhances (suppresses) the antiskyrmion speed while simultaneously reducing its Hall angle, thereby overcoming a key challenge for antiskyrmion racetrack memories. Our work establishes the intrinsic current lensing as a powerful mechanism for manipulating topological magnetic textures and opens new avenues for antiskyrmion-based spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: Antiskyrmions act as magnetic quadrupole lenses that focus or defocus electric currents, modifying current-induced antiskyrmion dynamics via spin-transfer torque and enabling a tunable, anisotropic quadrupolar antiskyrmion Hall effect.
AI.motivation: Antiskyrmion racetrack memories face a key challenge: undesirable Hall motion that deflects antiskyrmions away from the driving current direction, degrading device performance. A mechanism to control and mitigate this transverse deflection is needed.
AI.method: The authors use an iterative, self-consistent framework that couples quantum transport simulations with micromagnetic simulations to capture the coupled dynamics of conduction electrons and antiskyrmions, examining current focusing by the antiskyrmion core as a magnetic quadrupole lens and its back-action via spin-transfer torque.
AI.result: The antiskyrmion core acts as a focal point where electron beams converge for specific injection directions, producing anisotropic, nonuniform current distributions. This yields a quadrupolar antiskyrmion Hall effect that is highly anisotropic with respect to current direction and tunable by spin-orbit coupling. Current focusing (defocusing) strongly enhances (suppresses) antiskyrmion speed while simultaneously reducing its Hall angle.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic current lensing is established as a powerful mechanism for manipulating topological magnetic textures, overcoming a key challenge for antiskyrmion racetrack memories and opening new avenues for antiskyrmion-based spintronic devices.

title: Long-range self-avoiding walk in one dimension: a Monte Carlo study
summary: We study the one-dimensional long-range self-avoiding walk in the grand-canonical ensemble where the statistical weight of a jump of length $r$ decays algebraically as $r^{-(d+σ)}$. Using large-scale Monte Carlo simulations with an efficient irreversible update scheme, we obtain high-precision estimates of the critical fugacity $z_c$, the universal Binder ratio $Q_N^c$, the correlation-length exponent $ν$, and the anomalous dimension $η$. For $σ>1$, the critical fugacity varies smoothly with $σ$, while the Binder ratio and the critical exponents remain consistent with the short-range universality class. For $σ\le 1$, by contrast, the results clearly depart from short-range behavior, identifying $σ=1$ as the boundary between long-range and short-range regimes. In the long-range Wilson-Fisher regime with $1/2 < σ\leq 1$, $η$ agrees with the long-range Gaussian-fixed-point prediction $η_{\mathrm{GFP}}=2-σ$, whereas $Q_N^c$ and $ν$ vary nontrivially with $σ$ and exhibit discontinuous jumps at $σ=1$. These findings are in good agreement with the recently proposed universality diagram in the $(d,σ)$ plane for long-range O$(n)$ models, with the self-avoiding walk corresponding to the $n\to0$ limit.

AI.tldr: Monte Carlo study of 1D long-range self-avoiding walk finds σ=1 as the boundary between long-range and short-range universality, confirming the proposed (d,σ) universality diagram for O(n) models in the n→0 limit.
AI.motivation: To test the recently proposed universality diagram in the (d,σ) plane for long-range O(n) models by examining the one-dimensional long-range self-avoiding walk in the grand-canonical ensemble, where the jump weight decays as r^{-(d+σ)}.
AI.method: Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations using an efficient irreversible update scheme to obtain high-precision estimates of the critical fugacity z_c, the universal Binder ratio Q_N^c, the correlation-length exponent ν, and the anomalous dimension η.
AI.result: For σ>1, z_c varies smoothly with σ while Binder ratio and critical exponents match short-range universality. For σ≤1, results depart from short-range behavior, identifying σ=1 as the boundary. In the long-range Wilson-Fisher regime (1/2<σ≤1), η agrees with the Gaussian-fixed-point prediction η_GFP=2−σ, whereas Q_N^c and ν vary nontrivially with σ and show discontinuous jumps at σ=1.
AI.conclusion: The findings agree well with the proposed universality diagram in the (d,σ) plane for long-range O(n) models, with the self-avoiding walk corresponding to the n→0 limit.

title: Probing $d$-wave pairing in the $t$-$t'$-$U$ Hubbard model with tensor-backflow wave functions
summary: Building on the recently developed tensor-backflow method, which accurately describes energies and stripe states in the Fermi-Hubbard model, we investigate $d$-wave pairing in the two-dimensional $t$-$t'$-$U$ Hubbard model. For the $8\times8$ lattice, we improve the wave function using symmetry projections followed by one Lanczos step, whereas for the $12\times 12$ and $16\times 16$ lattices, we apply one Lanczos step without symmetry projection. We focus primarily on the parameter regime with filling $n=0.875$, on-site repulsion $U=8$ and next-nearest-neighbor hopping $t'=-0.2t$, a regime in which enhanced $d$-wave pairing has been reported. The resulting energies are competitive with those obtained using state-of-the-art neural quantum states. For example, on a $16\times 16$ lattice with periodic boundary conditions, the tensor-backflow wave function after one Lanczos step without explicit symmetry enforcement achieves a relative energy difference of $4.4\times 10^{-3}$ from the symmetry-preserving neural quantum state result. From the real space pair correlations, for $t'=-0.2t$, we observe stronger $d$-wave pair correlations together with the characteristic relative sign between horizontal and vertical bond-pair components. Compared with $t'=0$, finite negative $t'$ increases the spectral weight of the corresponding pair-density matrix, which indicates the enhanced overall $d$-wave pair fluctuations. The leading eigenvalue is enhanced on the $8\times8$ lattice for both with and without symmetry projections. For larger lattices such as $12\times 12$ and $16\times 16$, the leading pair-density matrix spectral weight is distributed among several nearly degenerate eigenmodes rather than being concentrated in a single dominant mode. This indicates enhanced and more broadly distributed $d$-wave pair fluctuations, but no single eigenvalue exhibits the extensive scaling required for ODLRO.

AI.tldr: Using the tensor-backflow method with a Lanczos step, this work computes $d$-wave pairing in the 2D $t$-$t'$-$U$ Hubbard model, finding energies competitive with state-of-the-art neural quantum states and enhanced, broadly distributed $d$-wave pair fluctuations at $t'=-0.2t$ without evidence of long-range order.
AI.motivation: The recently developed tensor-backflow method accurately describes energies and stripe states in the Fermi-Hubbard model, motivating its extension to study $d$-wave pairing in the 2D $t$-$t'$-$U$ Hubbard model, particularly in the regime ($n=0.875$, $U=8$, $t'=-0.2t$) where enhanced $d$-wave pairing has been reported.
AI.method: The wave function is improved by symmetry projections followed by one Lanczos step on the $8\times8$ lattice, and by one Lanczos step without symmetry projection on the $12\times12$ and $16\times16$ lattices. Pairing is characterized via real-space pair correlations and the pair-density matrix spectral weight.
AI.result: Energies are competitive with state-of-the-art neural quantum states; on a $16\times16$ lattice the tensor-backflow wave function after one Lanczos step achieves a relative energy difference of $4.4\times10^{-3}$ from the symmetry-preserving neural quantum state result. At $t'=-0.2t$, stronger $d$-wave pair correlations appear with the characteristic relative sign between horizontal and vertical bond-pair components. Finite negative $t'$ increases pair-density matrix spectral weight relative to $t'=0$, and the leading eigenvalue is enhanced on the $8\times8$ lattice (with and without symmetry projections). On $12\times12$ and $16\times16$ lattices, the leading spectral weight is distributed among several nearly degenerate eigenmodes.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate enhanced and more broadly distributed $d$-wave pair fluctuations at finite negative $t'$, but no single eigenvalue shows the extensive scaling required for off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO).

title: From Ferroionic Instability to Domain Patterns at an Exposed Surfaces of Multiaxial Ferroelectrics
summary: We analyze the formation of domain structures in multiaxial ferroelectrics with an open, electrochemically compensated surface. The model combines vector polarization, surface electrochemistry, electrostatics, compatible strain, and competitive adsorption on common sites. We construct homogeneous phase maps and analyze polarization instabilities, first assuming perturbations that are uniform through the film thickness and then allowing depth-dependent polarization profiles. Nonlinear continuation follows the growth of these modulations into developed domains. Optimization of their period and tests of their stability establish how the initial instability wavelength relates to the preferred spacing of an established domain structure. We also consider surface ordering above a stable, weakly anisotropic bulk as a constitutive limit relevant to ferroelectric relaxors, providing insight into possible origins of their periodic surface modulations. Surface energies with the same quadratic terms can produce the same initial instability but favor different developed states, including periodic domains and uniform in-plane polarization. This analysis provides a procedure for connecting the initial development of ferroelectric modulations to amplitude selection, wavelength adjustment, and the subsequent evolution of the resulting domain structures.

AI.tldr: This paper models domain structure formation in multiaxial ferroelectrics with open, electrochemically compensated surfaces, linking initial polarization instabilities to developed domain patterns via nonlinear continuation and stability analysis.
AI.motivation: Understanding how domain structures form in multiaxial ferroelectrics with open, electrochemically compensated surfaces, and how initial instabilities relate to final domain spacing, remains an open problem relevant to surface modulations and relaxor behavior.
AI.method: The model couples vector polarization, surface electrochemistry, electrostatics, compatible strain, and competitive adsorption on common sites. The authors construct homogeneous phase maps and analyze polarization instabilities first with thickness-uniform perturbations, then with depth-dependent polarization profiles. Nonlinear continuation tracks modulation growth into developed domains, with optimization of period and stability tests.
AI.result: Optimization and stability tests establish how the initial instability wavelength relates to the preferred spacing of the established domain structure. Surface ordering above a stable, weakly anisotropic bulk is examined as a constitutive limit relevant to relaxors. Surface energies sharing identical quadratic terms can yield the same initial instability yet favor different developed states, including periodic domains and uniform in-plane polarization.
AI.conclusion: The analysis provides a procedure connecting the initial development of ferroelectric modulations to amplitude selection, wavelength adjustment, and the subsequent evolution of the resulting domain structures.

title: ECENet: An Edge Cluster Expansion Line-Graph Neural Network
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a promising alternative to classical force fields and first-principles theory for predicting the properties of chemical and material systems. Many MLIPs are graph neural networks with O(3)-equivariant features, whose accuracy comes at substantial computational cost. Here we introduce the edge cluster expansion (ECE), an analogue of the atomic cluster expansion in which the environment is expanded around edges between atom pairs rather than single atoms, and build upon it to develop the line-graph neural network ECENet. ECENet uses O(2)-equivariant features that persist on the edges between atoms, giving it natural access to O(2) operations that are cheaper and less restrictive than their O(3) counterparts. ECENet performs at the state of the art on the MD22 benchmark and lies on the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier when trained on the SPICE-MACE-OFF dataset. Furthermore, with long-range electrostatics implemented via latent Ewald summation, ECENet accurately predicts molecular dipole moments and the infrared spectrum of liquid water. The frontier ECENet architecture establishes equivariant edge-centered representations as an efficient and physically expressive foundation for equivariant MLIPs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the edge cluster expansion (ECE) and ECENet, an O(2)-equivariant line-graph neural network MLIP that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on MD22 and Pareto-optimal accuracy-cost trade-offs, with applications to dipoles and IR spectra.
AI.motivation: MLIPs offer an alternative to classical force fields and first-principles methods, but many rely on O(3)-equivariant graph neural networks whose high accuracy incurs substantial computational cost. There is a need for more efficient, physically expressive architectures.
AI.method: The authors define the edge cluster expansion, an analogue of the atomic cluster expansion where the environment is expanded around atom-pair edges rather than single atoms. Building on it, they develop ECENet, a line-graph neural network using O(2)-equivariant features that persist on interatomic edges, giving access to cheaper and less restrictive O(2) operations than O(3) counterparts. Long-range electrostatics are implemented via latent Ewald summation.
AI.result: ECENet achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MD22 benchmark and lies on the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier when trained on SPICE-MACE-OFF. With latent Ewald summation, it accurately predicts molecular dipole moments and the infrared spectrum of liquid water.
AI.conclusion: The frontier ECENet architecture establishes equivariant edge-centered representations as an efficient and physically expressive foundation for equivariant MLIPs.

title: Gradient-estimator design overcomes trainability barriers in neural-network-based variational optimization
summary: Neural networks provide expressive representations for scientific computing. However, even sufficiently expressive networks can suffer training failure in weak-gradient regimes, limiting their practical use in quantum many-body physics and ab initio quantum chemistry. Here we derive an unbiased direct gradient estimator and introduce the adaptive minimum-variance phase (AMVP) estimator for neural-network variational optimization. By improving the signal-to-noise ratio of weak gradients, these methods enable reliable scientific calculations where training previously failed, while substantially reducing computational cost. The framework enables compact networks to outperform larger and fine-tuned default standard-estimator models with over an order of magnitude less GPU time on correlated flux models, and ultimately exceed the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) accuracy. It further achieves chemical accuracy in N$_2$ bond breaking and, for the first time, in heavy-element I$_2$ with explicit spin-orbit coupling. These results demonstrate that gradient-estimator design expands the capabilities of neural-network variational methods for accurate scientific computing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces unbiased direct gradient and adaptive minimum-variance phase (AMVP) estimators to fix training failure in weak-gradient regimes for neural-network variational optimization, achieving DMRG-level and chemical accuracy at far lower cost.
AI.motivation: Even sufficiently expressive neural networks can suffer training failure in weak-gradient regimes, limiting their practical use in quantum many-body physics and ab initio quantum chemistry.
AI.method: The authors derive an unbiased direct gradient estimator and introduce the adaptive minimum-variance phase (AMVP) estimator for neural-network variational optimization, improving the signal-to-noise ratio of weak gradients.
AI.result: Compact networks outperform larger, fine-tuned standard-estimator models with over an order of magnitude less GPU time on correlated flux models, exceed DMRG accuracy, and achieve chemical accuracy in N2 bond breaking and, for the first time, in heavy-element I2 with explicit spin-orbit coupling.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-estimator design expands the capabilities of neural-network variational methods for accurate scientific computing, enabling reliable calculations where training previously failed while substantially reducing computational cost.

title: Diff-NekRS: A Scalable Differentiable Framework for Multi-Timestep Solver-in-the-Loop Training
summary: Hybrid physics-machine-learning solvers improve under-resolved simulations by embedding trainable corrections into the time integration. During autoregressive inference, repeated solver-model interactions can amplify small errors, motivating multi-timestep solver-in-the-loop training. However, production solvers rarely expose the derivatives needed to backpropagate through such rollouts. We introduce Diff-NekRS, a scalable differentiable framework that embeds neural corrections directly in the GPU-accelerated NekRS incompressible-flow solver. NekRS computes the authoritative forward trajectory, a manually implemented exact discrete adjoint differentiates the supported fully discrete timestep, and LibTorch supplies neural vector-Jacobian products and parameter gradients. End-to-end Taylor and centered finite-difference tests verify the assembled gradient for two-dimensional cylinder flow (2Dcyl) and the three-dimensional Taylor-Green vortex (3DTGV) across five horizons and 12-1,020 MPI ranks. At 1,020 ranks, optimizer-enabled post-setup training updates retain 54.5%-78.0% and 80.7%-81.9% weak-scaling efficiency for 2Dcyl and 3DTGV, respectively. In 200-step autoregressive inference, the M = 50 model reduces the three-seed median terminal relative L2 velocity error by 59.2% for 2Dcyl and 12.1% for 3DTGV relative to the uncorrected coarse-grid P = 2 baseline, and retains wall-clock speedups of 5.38x and 2.49x, respectively, relative to the corresponding P = 7 configurations for equal simulated-time intervals. These results establish a verified and scalable path for multi-timestep solver-in-the-loop training that improves coarse-grid trajectory accuracy while retaining a speed advantage over the high-order reference

AI.tldr: Diff-NekRS is a scalable differentiable framework embedding neural corrections directly into the GPU-accelerated NekRS incompressible-flow solver, enabling multi-timestep solver-in-the-loop training via a manually implemented exact discrete adjoint and LibTorch-based neural VJPs, verified on 2D cylinder flow and 3D Taylor-Green vortex.
AI.motivation: Hybrid physics-ML solvers improve under-resolved simulations by embedding trainable corrections into time integration, but autoregressive inference amplifies small errors through repeated solver-model interactions, motivating multi-timestep solver-in-the-loop training. However, production solvers rarely expose the derivatives needed to backpropagate through such rollouts.
AI.method: Diff-NekRS computes the authoritative forward trajectory in NekRS, uses a manually implemented exact discrete adjoint to differentiate the supported fully discrete timestep, and uses LibTorch for neural vector-Jacobian products and parameter gradients. Gradients are verified with end-to-end Taylor and centered finite-difference tests for 2D cylinder flow (2Dcyl) and the 3D Taylor-Green vortex (3DTGV) across five horizons and 12-1,020 MPI ranks.
AI.result: At 1,020 ranks, optimizer-enabled post-setup training updates retain 54.5%-78.0% and 80.7%-81.9% weak-scaling efficiency for 2Dcyl and 3DTGV. In 200-step autoregressive inference, the M = 50 model reduces three-seed median terminal relative L2 velocity error by 59.2% for 2Dcyl and 12.1% for 3DTGV relative to the uncorrected coarse-grid P = 2 baseline, while retaining wall-clock speedups of 5.38x and 2.49x over equivalent P = 7 configurations for equal simulated-time intervals.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a verified and scalable path for multi-timestep solver-in-the-loop training that improves coarse-grid trajectory accuracy while retaining a speed advantage over the high-order reference.

title: Magnetic Particle Magnetometer Based on Langevin Response of Superparamagnetic Nanoparticles for Remote Magnetic Field Sensing
summary: We demonstrate a novel magnetometer that utilizes the Langevin nonlinear magnetization of superparamagnetic nanoparticles as the sensing medium. The magnetic sensor exploits the even-order harmonics of the magnetization response, particularly the second harmonic, which is proportional to the local magnetic field component. By remotely detecting the magnetization response, the magnetometer enables non-invasive, localized, and distributed magnetic field sensing without requiring wired connections, with a small sensing volume, which can be used for in situ biomedical sensing, geomagnetic monitoring, smart diagnostics, and distributed industrial sensing. In the linear operating regime, the magnetometer provides a measurement range of $\pm$ 0.2 mT and a high sensitivity of 10 pT/$\sqrt{Hz}$, while an extended operating mode allows measurements over a range exceeding $\pm$ 0.5 mT. The sensor offers a dynamic bandwidth from dc up to a few kilohertz, determined by the excitation frequency.

AI.tldr: A novel magnetometer using the Langevin nonlinear magnetization of superparamagnetic nanoparticles as the sensing medium, exploiting even-order (second) harmonics for remote, non-invasive, localized magnetic field sensing, achieving 10 pT/√Hz sensitivity, ±0.2 mT linear range (extendable beyond ±0.5 mT), and dc-to-kilohertz bandwidth.
AI.motivation: Conventional magnetometers typically require wired connections and offer limited flexibility for localized, distributed, or in situ magnetic field sensing. There is a need for a non-invasive, wirelessly detectable, small-volume magnetic sensing approach suitable for applications such as biomedical sensing, geomagnetic monitoring, smart diagnostics, and distributed industrial sensing.
AI.method: The magnetometer uses superparamagnetic nanoparticles as the sensing medium and exploits their Langevin nonlinear magnetization. It detects even-order harmonics of the magnetization response, particularly the second harmonic, which is proportional to the local magnetic field component. The magnetization response is detected remotely, eliminating the need for wired connections and enabling a small sensing volume.
AI.result: In the linear operating regime, the magnetometer achieves a measurement range of ±0.2 mT with a sensitivity of 10 pT/√Hz; an extended operating mode covers a range exceeding ±0.5 mT. The dynamic bandwidth spans from dc up to a few kilohertz, determined by the excitation frequency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed nanoparticle-based magnetometer enables non-invasive, localized, and distributed magnetic field sensing without wired connections and with a small sensing volume. It is potentially applicable to in situ biomedical sensing, geomagnetic monitoring, smart diagnostics, and distributed industrial sensing.

title: Coexistence and Interconversion of Multiple-Order Majorana Modes in Topological Superconductor Films with Varying Thickness
summary: We theoretically investigate the thickness-dependent evolution of Majorana modes in $C_{2h}$-symmetric topological superconductor films (such as the recently discovered 2M-WS$_2$) proximity coupled with magnetic insulators. For sufficiently thick films, two Majorana bound states coexist as end modes at the surface and interface along a vortex line, with the interfacial mode evolving into a chiral Majorana edge mode upon increasing the proximity-induced exchange field. The intrinsic $C_{2h}$ crystalline symmetry selects two chiral Majorana modes circulating along the hinges on two of the four side surfaces of the film. When the penetration depth of the exchange field is sufficiently shallow, the two circulating modes are localized near the interface, but with qualitatively different subsequent evolutions. One of them further collapses to form two Majorana corner modes, while the other merges with the chiral Majorana mode circulating around the interface. Importantly, the corner modes are well decoupled from the interfacial chiral mode, thereby enabling an unprecedented coexistence of first-, second-, and third-order Majorana modes within a single material platform. We further show that such coexistence persists even in the ultrathin-film limit, where the electric-field-controlled two-dimensional $Z_2$ topology offers an extra advantage to readily interconvert the multiple-order Majorana modes. These findings highlight the pivotal role of the proper crystalline symmetry in enabling emergence, manipulation, and potential braiding of Majorana modes for demonstrating non-Abelian statistics and fault-tolerant quantum computation.

AI.tldr: This work predicts that $C_{2h}$-symmetric topological superconductor films (e.g., 2M-WS$_2$) proximity coupled to magnetic insulators host coexisting first-, second-, and third-order Majorana modes in one platform, controllable by film thickness and exchange field.
AI.motivation: Realizing and manipulating Majorana modes of different orders (bound, chiral edge, and corner modes) typically requires distinct material platforms, hindering braiding and non-Abelian statistics demonstration. A single tunable system hosting coexisting multiple-order Majorana modes is desired.
AI.method: Theoretical investigation of thickness-dependent evolution of Majorana modes in $C_{2h}$-symmetric topological superconductor films proximity coupled with magnetic insulators, analyzing the role of intrinsic crystalline symmetry, penetration depth of the exchange field, and electric-field-controlled 2D $Z_2$ topology in the ultrathin limit.
AI.result: For thick films, two Majorana bound states coexist as surface and interface end modes along a vortex line, the interfacial one becoming a chiral Majorana edge mode under increasing exchange field. $C_{2h}$ symmetry selects two chiral Majorana modes along hinges on two side surfaces. With shallow exchange-field penetration, one collapses into two Majorana corner modes while the other merges with the interfacial chiral mode; the corner modes decouple from the interfacial chiral mode, yielding coexistence of first-, second-, and third-order Majorana modes. This coexistence persists in the ultrathin-film limit.
AI.conclusion: Proper crystalline symmetry is pivotal for enabling emergence, manipulation, and potential braiding of multiple-order Majorana modes, offering a route toward non-Abelian statistics and fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Collective depinning of dipolar skyrmion chains: thermal and athermal rounding of an elastic polymer in a quenched landscape
summary: The dynamics of interacting dipole skyrmion chains in a weak pinning landscape is studied through numerical solutions of the stochastic Thiele equation. Chains of different lengths with periodic boundary conditions are driven across quenched attractive pinning sites under different magnetic fields. A clear threshold spin current is identified as the critical depinning force. Three main results emerge: (i) for chains of 50 skyrmions or more, the depinning threshold is independent of chain length and remains close to one third of that of an isolated skyrmion. (ii) The transition rounding is only partly thermal: the width changes from w = 0.334 +/- 0.004 decades at T = 0 to 0.633 +/- 0.002 at 300 K, while the intrinsic Larkin correlation length remains about 2.6 bonds below kBT ~ V0/25. (iii) The width is nearly unchanged up to kBT ~ 0.14 V0, but increases almost fourfold by kBT ~ 0.23 V0, mainly through broadening of the creep regime. It is independent of chain length, ruling out finite-size rounding. Increasing the field from 30 to 40 mT changes the transition shape, widening its core by 26% while shortening the creep tails. For chains of about 200 skyrmions, depinning proceeds through a sequence of internal deformations - growth of the Larkin length and roughness, transient bond stretching, and subsequent recovery of mobility and Hall angle. These collective effects are relevant for skyrmion-based devices in which chains, rather than isolated textures, act as information carriers.

AI.tldr: Numerical study of dipole skyrmion chains depinning in weak pinning landscape via stochastic Thiele equation, revealing length-independent threshold, partial thermal rounding, and collective deformation-driven depinning.
AI.motivation: Skyrmion-based devices may use chains rather than isolated textures as information carriers, so understanding how interacting skyrmion chains depin collectively in a weak pinning landscape is essential.
AI.method: Stochastic Thiele equation simulations of interacting dipole skyrmion chains with periodic boundary conditions, driven across quenched attractive pinning sites under varying magnetic fields and thermal conditions.
AI.result: (i) For chains of 50+ skyrmions, depinning threshold is length-independent and ~1/3 that of an isolated skyrmion. (ii) Rounding is only partly thermal: width grows from 0.334±0.004 decades at T=0 to 0.633±0.002 at 300 K; Larkin length stays ~2.6 bonds below kBT ~ V0/25. (iii) Width nearly constant up to kBT ~ 0.14 V0, then increases ~4-fold by kBT ~ 0.23 V0 via creep broadening, independent of chain length. Field increase 30→40 mT widens transition core by 26% while shortening creep tails. For ~200-skyrmion chains, depinning proceeds through growth of Larkin length and roughness, transient bond stretching, then recovery of mobility and Hall angle.
AI.conclusion: Collective effects govern skyrmion chain depinning, with a length-independent threshold and thermal rounding that is only partly thermal; these findings are relevant for skyrmion-based devices using chains as information carriers.

title: Critical Touching of Temporal Entanglement Transitions
summary: Equilibrium phase transitions are conventionally categorized into first-order and continuous phase transitions. Far from equilibrium, many new transitions emerge during the real-time evolution of quantum systems. One such transition is the temporal entanglement transition (TET) characterized by the nonanalyticity of the entanglement spectrum. So far, all TETs occur through a linear crossing of the leading Schmidt levels in different symmetry sectors, resembling a first-order transition in equilibrium. A natural question is whether a continuous TET, featured by entanglement spectrum touching, is possible. In a periodically driven transverse $J_1$-$J_2$ Ising chain, we show that two such TETs can merge into a critical touching, where the leading levels meet tangentially without exchanging, realizing the temporal analog of a continuous phase transition. Near the critical frequency, the temporal separation of the two TETs vanishes continuously and its derivative with respect to frequency diverges, a nonanalytic signature that is absent in a single first-order TET. This finite-frequency touching arises from the interplay between a weak symmetry-preserving perturbation of the product initial state and Floquet corrections. Further extending the frequency scan reveals a second critical touching at a higher frequency, and the two critical frequencies enclose a finite window with no TET. These features can be understood from a second-order Floquet Hamiltonian and persist across a broad range of coupling ratios, establishing the critical touching as a distinct form of TET.

AI.tldr: In a periodically driven transverse J1-J2 Ising chain, two temporal entanglement transitions (TETs) can merge into a critical touching where leading Schmidt levels meet tangentially without crossing, realizing a temporal analog of a continuous phase transition with nonanalytic signatures near the critical frequency.
AI.motivation: All known temporal entanglement transitions occur via a linear crossing of leading Schmidt levels in different symmetry sectors, resembling equilibrium first-order transitions. Whether a continuous TET, characterized by entanglement spectrum touching, is possible remained an open question.
AI.method: The authors study a periodically driven transverse J1-J2 Ising chain, examining the real-time evolution of the entanglement spectrum and the behavior of the leading Schmidt levels under frequency scans, supported by a second-order Floquet Hamiltonian analysis.
AI.result: Two TETs are shown to merge into a critical touching where leading levels meet tangentially without exchanging. Near the critical frequency, the temporal separation of the two TETs vanishes continuously and its frequency derivative diverges. A second critical touching appears at higher frequency, and the two critical frequencies enclose a finite window with no TET. These features persist across a broad range of coupling ratios.
AI.conclusion: The critical touching constitutes a distinct form of TET, realizing the temporal analog of a continuous phase transition driven by the interplay between a weak symmetry-preserving perturbation of the product initial state and Floquet corrections.

title: On the precise boundary of the Néel antiferromagnetic phase in the Shastry-Sutherland model
comment: Main text: 6 pages, 4 figures. Supplemental Materials: 9 pages, 9 figures
summary: The ground state phase diagram of the Shastry-Sutherland model remains controversial. In particular, the nature of the transition between the plaquette valence bond solid (PVBS) phase and the Néel antiferromagnetic (AFM) phase is still under debate. While some studies suggest a direct transition between the two phases, others propose the existence of a narrow intermediate quantum spin liquid regime. To address this issue, we perform large-scale Density Matrix Renormalization Group calculations to determine the Néel AFM phase boundary in the Shastry-Sutherland model. By applying staggered boundary pinning fields and directly measuring the bulk staggered magnetization, and through systematic extrapolations with respect to truncation error as well as careful finite-size scaling, we find that the staggered magnetization remains finite across the controversial region $0.78 \lesssim J_{1}/J_{2} \leq 0.81$, which was suggested to host a quantum spin liquid phase in some studies. Together with the previously established consensus placing the PVBS phase boundary at $J_{1}/J_{2} \approx 0.78$, these results provide evidence against the existence of an intermediate quantum spin liquid phase and support a direct PVBS--Néel AFM transition in the Shastry-Sutherland model.

AI.tldr: Large-scale DMRG calculations with staggered boundary pinning fields and extrapolation to zero truncation error show the bulk staggered magnetization remains finite up to J1/J2 ≈ 0.81, ruling out an intermediate quantum spin liquid and supporting a direct PVBS–Néel transition in the Shastry-Sutherland model.
AI.motivation: The ground-state phase diagram of the Shastry-Sutherland model is controversial: it is debated whether the plaquette valence bond solid (PVBS) and Néel antiferromagnetic (AFM) phases are separated by a direct transition or by a narrow intermediate quantum spin liquid regime. Resolving this requires an accurate determination of the Néel AFM phase boundary.
AI.method: Large-scale Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) calculations. The bulk staggered magnetization is measured directly under staggered boundary pinning fields, with systematic extrapolations in truncation error and careful finite-size scaling.
AI.result: The staggered magnetization remains finite across the controversial region 0.78 ≲ J1/J2 ≤ 0.81, previously proposed to host a quantum spin liquid. Combined with the established PVBS boundary at J1/J2 ≈ 0.78, this leaves no window for an intermediate spin liquid.
AI.conclusion: The results provide evidence against an intermediate quantum spin liquid phase and support a direct PVBS–Néel AFM transition in the Shastry-Sutherland model.

title: A Hybrid Quantum Neural Network to Analyse Big Experimental Powder X-ray Diffraction Data
summary: Quantitative analysis of experimental powder X-ray diffraction data remains challenging when evaluating complex multiphase materials and noisy measurements. We introduce a hybrid quantum neural network framework designed to extract quantitative parameters, such as phase weight fractions and scale factors, directly from one-dimensional powder diffraction patterns without iterative refinement. The model combines noise-aware classical simulator pre-training with fast downstream fine-tuning on quantum processing unit features, ensuring stability against hardware decoherence. We demonstrate the practical utility of this approach by deploying the trained network onto an IBM quantum computer to analyse experimental X-ray diffraction computed tomography datasets from a three-phase solid oxide fuel cell containing ca. 10,000 patterns and a four-phase lithium-ion battery containing ca. 20,000 patterns). The network successfully reconstructs quantitative spatial phase maps in strong agreement with classical Rietveld refinement, paving the way for using quantum computing hardware to analyse real-world materials characterisation data.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum neural network extracts quantitative phase parameters directly from 1D powder XRD patterns, avoiding iterative refinement, and is deployed on IBM quantum hardware to reconstruct spatial phase maps from large experimental XRD-CT datasets of solid oxide fuel cell and lithium-ion battery samples, matching classical Rietveld refinement.
AI.motivation: Quantitative analysis of experimental powder X-ray diffraction data is challenging for complex multiphase materials and noisy measurements; conventional approaches rely on iterative refinement, which is computationally costly and difficult at scale.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum neural network combines noise-aware classical simulator pre-training with downstream fine-tuning on quantum processing unit features to ensure stability against hardware decoherence, learning to predict phase weight fractions and scale factors directly from one-dimensional powder diffraction patterns without iterative refinement.
AI.result: Deployed on an IBM quantum computer, the trained network analysed experimental XRD-CT datasets: a three-phase solid oxide fuel cell (~10,000 patterns) and a four-phase lithium-ion battery (~20,000 patterns), successfully reconstructing quantitative spatial phase maps in strong agreement with classical Rietveld refinement.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that quantum computing hardware can be applied to analyse real-world materials characterisation data, paving the way for quantum-accelerated quantitative diffraction analysis.

title: Solvent Inertia Changes Product Probability by Relocating the Phase-Space Reactivity Boundary
comment: 10 pages, including 5 pages of Supplementary Material; 1 main figure and 1 supplementary figure. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22852306
summary: Changing solvent inertia changes the kinetic part of a molecular Hamiltonian and hence its flow in phase space, without requiring a change in the potential energy surface (PES). We study how this affects product probability in a solute-solvent model with two degrees of freedom. Initial conditions are chosen at the same total energy for each solvent mass. For this family, the deterministic outcome changes from reaching products to returning to reactants at a threshold mass. The initial condition at that mass belongs to the stable manifold of the transition-state periodic orbit. Weak Gaussian forcing of the solvent momentum replaces the abrupt change in outcome by a continuous change in product probability over a mass interval proportional to the square root of the noise strength. The deterministic threshold and a linear response calculation predict the position and width of this probability change without fitting the stochastic simulations. Monte Carlo results at three noise strengths agree with the prediction within sampling uncertainty. The calculation connects solvent inertia to product probability through the geometry of the full Hamiltonian flow, rather than through a change in the PES.

AI.tldr: Solvent inertia alters the kinetic term of a solute-solvent Hamiltonian, shifting product probability via phase-space geometry rather than PES changes; noise smooths the deterministic threshold over a width scaling as sqrt(noise strength), and a linear-response/Langer-type calculation predicts this shift and width without fitting.
AI.motivation: Solvent dynamics are often assumed to influence reactions through the potential energy surface (e.g., friction, dielectric effects). This work asks whether changing solvent inertia alone—altering only the kinetic part of the Hamiltonian—can control reactivity, thereby isolating a purely mechanical (phase-space flow) route from electronic/PES effects.
AI.method: A minimal two-degree-of-freedom solute-solvent model Hamiltonian. Initial conditions sampled at fixed total energy across a family of solvent masses. Deterministic trajectories analyzed via transition-state periodic orbit and its stable manifold. Weak Gaussian noise added to solvent momentum (Monte Carlo simulations at three noise strengths). Linear response theory with the deterministic threshold used to predict the position and width of the stochastic product-probability transition.
AI.result: Deterministic outcome switches from products to reactants at a threshold solvent mass; at threshold the initial condition lies on the stable manifold of the transition-state periodic orbit. Noise converts this discontinuous switch into a sigmoidal probability change over a mass interval scaling as the square root of noise strength. Predicted transition position and width match Monte Carlo results within sampling uncertainty for three noise strengths.
AI.conclusion: Solvent inertia can tune product probability through the geometry of the full Hamiltonian phase-space flow, independent of any PES modification. The deterministic threshold plus linear response suffices to predict stochastic product probabilities without fitting, linking solvent mass to reactivity in a parameter-free way.

title: Extreme-Scale Ising Machines with Cluster Mean-Field Theory
summary: Scaling analog and digital Ising machines to larger problems requires overcoming finite device capacity and the cost of communication between devices. We present cluster mean-field theory (CMFT), a framework that partitions a large interaction graph into clusters sized to fit available hardware. Each cluster performs local updates independently, while interactions across cluster boundaries enter through periodically updated effective biases computed from boundary-spin averages. To reduce the error introduced by fixed cluster boundaries, we introduce dynamic partitioning, which cycles through multiple partitions so that interactions approximated by mean fields at one stage can act through instantaneous spins at another. On three-dimensional spin glasses and planted Pegasus instances, dynamic CMFT exhibits power-law decay of residual energy over sweep budgets. This shows that solution quality continues to improve with computational effort despite the mean-field approximation. An automated graph partitioner combined with a weighted recovery ratio provides a practical heuristic for selecting partition combinations on graphs without natural cut directions. We demonstrate CMFT on four GPUs with approximately four million p-bits, reaching comparable energy densities up to 15 times faster than a single-GPU implementation of the full graph. By coupling locally evolving clusters through programmable effective biases, CMFT provides a route to extreme-scale Ising machines on both analog and digital hardware.

AI.tldr: CMFT partitions a large Ising interaction graph into hardware-sized clusters updated locally, with cross-cluster interactions handled via periodically refreshed effective mean-field biases; dynamic partitioning cycles through multiple partitions to reduce boundary error, enabling extreme-scale Ising machines with power-law improvement in solution quality.
AI.motivation: Scaling analog and digital Ising machines to larger problems is limited by finite device capacity and inter-device communication costs, so a framework is needed to decompose large graphs while retaining solution quality.
AI.method: Cluster mean-field theory (CMFT) partitions the interaction graph into clusters sized to fit available hardware. Clusters update locally and independently, while inter-cluster interactions enter through periodically updated effective biases computed from boundary-spin averages. Dynamic partitioning cycles through multiple partitions so mean-field-approximated interactions at one stage act through instantaneous spins at another. An automated graph partitioner with a weighted recovery ratio heuristic selects partition combinations on graphs lacking natural cut directions. Implementation uses four GPUs with ~4 million p-bits.
AI.result: On three-dimensional spin glasses and planted Pegasus instances, dynamic CMFT shows power-law decay of residual energy over sweep budgets, indicating solution quality keeps improving with computational effort despite the mean-field approximation. On four GPUs with ~4 million p-bits, it reaches comparable energy densities up to 15x faster than a single-GPU full-graph implementation.
AI.conclusion: Coupling locally evolving clusters through programmable effective biases makes CMFT a viable route to extreme-scale Ising machines on both analog and digital hardware.

title: MadVfold: accelerating NLO event generation and reducing negative weights with SIMD vectorization and GPUs
summary: NLO simulations are essential for LHC physics analyses but are expensive, as they are not only slow but also lead to negative weights, which imply the need to simulate much larger samples of events. Folding is a powerful technique to reduce negative weights but is itself expensive. In this paper I propose ``vectorized folding'' as a new idea to speed up these calculations using SIMD and GPUs, and I present its CUDACPP-based implementation for MG5aMC in MadVfold, including its extension for unfolded NLO event generation. Preliminary results show overall speedups around 6x to 9x with folding and 3x without it. This work is based on a test-centric, LLM-assisted software development process.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "vectorized folding," a SIMD/GPU-accelerated technique implemented as MadVfold (CUDACPP-based) for MG5aMC, achieving ~6–9x speedup with folding and ~3x without it for NLO simulations.
AI.motivation: NLO simulations are essential for LHC physics analyses but computationally expensive: they are slow and produce negative weights, which necessitate simulating much larger event samples. Folding reduces negative weights but is itself costly, so faster calculations are needed.
AI.method: The author proposes "vectorized folding" to accelerate these calculations using SIMD and GPUs, and presents a CUDACPP-based implementation for MG5aMC in MadVfold, including an extension for unfolded NLO event generation. The development process is test-centric and LLM-assisted.
AI.result: Preliminary results show overall speedups of approximately 6x to 9x with folding and about 3x without folding.
AI.conclusion: Vectorized folding via SIMD/GPU acceleration (MadVfold) substantially speeds up NLO simulations, addressing the cost of folding and negative weights, with promising preliminary speedups.

title: Temporal Quadrupole Moments: Floquet Higher-Order Topology with Nonreciprocal Frequency-Converting Corner States
summary: We introduce the temporal quadrupole moment and leverage its nonreciprocal frequency-converting topological corner states to experimentally realize a magnet-free transceiving circulator in a topological time-modulated microwave metasurface. Under periodic driving, the temporal quadrupole moment evolves the corner charge of a bulk-gapped lattice over the drive cycle, generating two distinct families of topologically protected corner states: a corner mode at quasienergy $\varepsilon=0$ and a purely dynamical period-doubled mode at $\varepsilon=π/T$ that exists only under periodic driving. We show that the relative phase between the two time-modulated coupling channels that generate it acts as a synthetic gauge field, breaking time-reversal symmetry while leaving the corner-mode topological protection intact. Specifically, a signal launched into the metasurface at TX port at frequency is up-converted and radiated into free space, while a free-space wave at is preferentially captured and routed --- at the same frequency, unconverted --- to RX port rather than back to TX port; the reverse itinerary is forbidden by the same broken symmetry. We confirm the temporal quadrupole moment, its associated Floquet corner states, and the resulting nonreciprocal frequency conversion through spatial field-intensity and angle-resolved radiation measurements of the time-modulated array on a fabricated microwave prototype.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a temporal quadrupole moment and use its nonreciprocal frequency-converting Floquet corner states to build a magnet-free transceiving circulator in a time-modulated microwave metasurface.
AI.motivation: Conventional circulators rely on magnetic materials and external bias magnets, which are bulky and incompatible with integrated, chip-scale, or magnet-free platforms. Topological time-modulated systems offer a route to nonreciprocity without magnetic bias, but a concrete topological quantity and corner-state mechanism enabling frequency-converting nonreciprocal routing had not been experimentally demonstrated.
AI.method: The work defines a temporal quadrupole moment for a periodically driven bulk-gapped lattice, showing it drives the corner charge over the drive cycle and yields two families of topologically protected corner states: a quasienergy-zero mode and a purely dynamical period-doubled mode at ε=π/T. The relative phase between the two time-modulated coupling channels serves as a synthetic gauge field that breaks time-reversal symmetry while preserving the corner-mode topological protection. A fabricated topological time-modulated microwave metasurface prototype is characterized via spatial field-intensity mapping and angle-resolved radiation measurements.
AI.result: A signal injected at the TX port is up-converted in frequency and radiated into free space, while a free-space wave is preferentially captured and routed to the RX port at the same unconverted frequency rather than back to TX; the reverse itinerary is forbidden by the broken symmetry. The temporal quadrupole moment, its associated Floquet corner states, and the resulting nonreciprocal frequency conversion are confirmed experimentally.
AI.conclusion: The temporal quadrupole moment provides a viable topological design principle for magnet-free nonreciprocal devices. Its Floquet corner states experimentally realize a frequency-converting transceiving circulator in a time-modulated microwave metasurface, establishing a route toward compact, magnet-free circulators and topological time-modulated photonic/microwave components.

title: Parallel Simulation of Josephson Junctions With Multiplicative Noise
summary: Parallel graphic processing units have been employed for fast simulations of the switching dynam- ics of Josephson junctions subject to critical current fluctuations. Such a system is modeled by a nonequilibrium washboard model with multiplicative noise, for which analytical results are lacking. The proposed approach allows us to execute extensive numerical simulation in short time and with relatively inexpensive resources. This allows us to fully characterize the effect of the noise on the junction switching current distributions at realistic bias current sweeprates.

AI.tldr: GPU parallelization enables fast, low-cost extensive simulations of Josephson junction switching dynamics under critical current fluctuations, fully characterizing noise effects on switching current distributions at realistic sweep rates.
AI.motivation: The switching dynamics of Josephson junctions subject to critical current fluctuations are modeled by a nonequilibrium washboard model with multiplicative noise, for which analytical results are unavailable, necessitating extensive numerical simulation.
AI.method: Parallel graphics processing units (GPUs) are employed to perform large-scale numerical simulations of the nonequilibrium washboard model with multiplicative noise at realistic bias current sweep rates.
AI.result: Extensive numerical simulations are executed in short time with relatively inexpensive resources, allowing full characterization of the noise effect on the junction switching current distributions at realistic bias current sweep rates.
AI.conclusion: GPU-based parallel simulation provides an efficient and cost-effective route to characterize multiplicative-noise effects on Josephson junction switching current distributions where analytical treatments are lacking.

title: Non-Markovian Quantum Dynamics of Exciton-Polaritons
summary: Exciton-polaritons, hybrid light-matter quasiparticles formed when a material interacts with a confined electric field, have experimentally been shown to exhibit mesoscale coherent quantum propagation that remains robust at room temperature. However, an accurate and direct quantum dynamical simulation of this phenomenon that does not resort to semi-classical approximations is prohibitively expensive computationally, limiting the microscopic understanding of the rich dynamical interplay among phonons, photons, and electrons under collective light-matter coupling. To address this fundamental challenge, we develop a non-Markovian master equation approach which enables the fully quantum mechanical simulation of non-equilibrium exciton-polariton dynamics and captures phonon-induced decoherence and dissipation beyond the conventional Markovian limit. To carry out this task, a procedure is developed in which the wave vector space is coarse-grained and each diagonal element of the density matrix is evolved in parallel. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we simulate exciton-polariton transport in TIPS-pentacene. We find that our approach reasonably captures the experimentally observed renormalization of the polariton group velocity, which originates from the phonon-induced non-Markovian Lamb shift. We further show that this renormalization cannot be reproduced within conventional Markovian theories.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a non-Markovian master equation approach for fully quantum mechanical simulation of non-equilibrium exciton-polariton dynamics, using wave vector space coarse-graining and parallel density matrix evolution, validated on TIPS-pentacene transport.
AI.motivation: Exciton-polaritons exhibit mesoscale coherent quantum propagation robust at room temperature, but accurate direct quantum dynamical simulation without semiclassical approximations is prohibitively expensive, limiting microscopic understanding of the interplay among phonons, photons, and electrons under collective light-matter coupling.
AI.method: A non-Markovian master equation approach enabling fully quantum mechanical simulation of non-equilibrium exciton-polariton dynamics, capturing phonon-induced decoherence and dissipation beyond the Markovian limit. Wave vector space is coarse-grained and each diagonal element of the density matrix is evolved in parallel.
AI.result: Simulations of exciton-polariton transport in TIPS-pentacene reasonably capture the experimentally observed renormalization of the polariton group velocity, originating from the phonon-induced non-Markovian Lamb shift. This renormalization cannot be reproduced within conventional Markovian theories.
AI.conclusion: The non-Markovian master equation approach offers a computationally tractable route to fully quantum simulation of exciton-polariton dynamics, revealing that non-Markovian Lamb shifts are essential for reproducing experimentally observed group velocity renormalization.

title: Rank-dependent optimal resetting in multiparticle search
summary: In many soft-matter and biological systems, task completion relies on the cumulative arrival of multiple searchers rather than the speed of a single pioneer. The completion kinetics are therefore set not only by the first arrival, but by the full ordered sequence of first-passage times. Here, we determine how stochastic resetting optimizes these ordered arrivals for all arrival ranks. We construct an exact finite-$N$ reference for non-interacting Brownian searchers and obtain the mean ordered first-passage time $\langle T_{(k)} \rangle$ and its optimal resetting rate $r_k^*$. For searchers with identical initial conditions, $r_k^*$ increases monotonically with arrival rank and, with increasing population size, approaches the known large-$N$ quantile limit where a finite optimum appears only above a critical rank fraction $φ_c \simeq 0.412$. Spatial heterogeneity qualitatively reorganizes this sequence, shifting its maximum from late to early ranks even without particle interactions. We then compare this baseline with Brownian colloid experiments, interacting active Brownian particles, and a collective autochemotactic search with persistent environmental memory. Across these systems, sensitivity to resetting increases strongly with arrival rank, while deviations from appropriate non-interacting references reveal the influence of direct interactions, finite return overhead, and environmental memory. Our results show that optimal resetting in multiparticle search is governed by the required completion rank and must be evaluated relative to protocol- and geometry-matched baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper derives exact finite-N results for how stochastic resetting optimizes the ordered first-passage times of multiple searchers, showing that the optimal resetting rate grows with arrival rank and that heterogeneity, interactions, and memory systematically modify this baseline.
AI.motivation: Many soft-matter and biological tasks require the cumulative arrival of multiple searchers rather than a single fast pioneer, so the relevant kinetics are governed not by the first arrival but by the full ordered sequence of first-passage times. Prior understanding of resetting-optimized search was largely limited to first arrival or single-searcher settings, leaving unclear how resetting should be tuned for completion ranks.
AI.method: The authors build an exact finite-N reference model of non-interacting Brownian searchers and analytically obtain the mean ordered first-passage time ⟨T_(k)⟩ and its optimal resetting rate r_k*. They then compare this reference against Brownian colloid experiments, interacting active Brownian particles, and a collective autochemotactic search model with persistent environmental memory.
