title: Transitions between bulk and interfacial fracture in diamond/$c$BN heterostructures
summary: Whether an initially crack-free heterostructure fails at its interface or within an adjoining phase is controlled by the relative cohesion of competing atomic planes, but how interfacial chemistry, crystallographic orientation, and intermixing reshape this competition remains unclear. Here, we combine density functional theory (DFT) with a fine-tuned atomistic foundation model to resolve tensile fracture in coherent diamond/cubic boron nitride (cBN) heterostructures. The resulting potential reproduces independent DFT tensile responses, including an unseen (001) interface orientation. Interfacial termination, orientation, and diffusion-induced intermixing jointly determine fracture resistance and fracture-plane selection. C-N-bonded (111) and C-B-bonded (001) remain interface-controlled throughout the investigated intermixing range, whereas pristine C-B-bonded (111) fractures at a neighboring B-N plane inside cBN because the interface is more strongly bound. Increasing the diffusion fraction from 0 to 50.0% causes a nonlinear decrease in fracture strength from 50.3 to 15.8 GPa and drives a bulk-to-interface transition through three regimes: cBN fracture up to 4.86%, configuration-dependent competition between 7.6 and 10.1%, and interfacial fracture at 12.5% and above. Atom-resolved stress fields and DFT separation energetics show that this transition is associated with stress relocation and a reversal in the relative cohesion of competing planes, while electron localization analysis connects the cohesion hierarchy to termination- and orientation-dependent bonding. These results establish an atomistic framework for controlling fracture resistance and fracture pathways in strongly bonded heterostructures.

title: Ferroelectric switching of odd-parity magnon spin splitting
summary: Magnetic symmetry can lift spin degeneracy in momentum space without producing net magnetization, generating spin textures classified by their parity under momentum reversal. Even-parity textures have well established in altermagnets. Odd-parity spin textures have recently emerged in electronic bands of compensated magnets, but their counterpart in collective bosonic excitations remains experimentally unresolved. Magnons provide a natural setting for this extension because they carry spin angular momentum through insulating magnets without accompanying charge flow. Beyond realizing this missing state, a broader challenge is to program spin splitting with voltage at room temperature. Here we report room-temperature transport evidence for ferroelectric switching odd-parity magnon spin splitting in multiferroic BiFeO3. Symmetry analysis and spin-wave calculations reveal that the cycloidal chirality splits opposite-spin magnon branches with an odd-in-momentum dependence and sets the sign. Experimentally, an injected in-plane-polarized spin current generates an out-of-plane magnon spin component during propagation. This component exhibits the crystalline angular dependence predicted by theory and reverses upon ferroelectric switching, providing a transport fingerprint of the spin-split magnon state. We use the programmed magnon spin to drive deterministic field-free switching of a perpendicular ferromagnet and demonstrate XNOR logic-in-memory. Our results extend odd-parity spin splitting from fermionic electronic states to bosonic collective modes and establish nonvolatile electrical control at room temperature.

Beyond realizing this missing bosonic state, a broader challenge is to program spin splitting with voltage at room temperature.

title: Charge-4e Superconducting Ground State without Pair Condensation: Exact Quartet Dynamics, Rigorous Order, and a Microscopic Route
summary: A direct charge-\(4e\) superconductor exhibits coherent four-electron order while every charge-\(2e\) pairing channel remains uncondensed. We establish three complementary results. First, building on the \(η\)-clustering states and bipartite parent of Yoshida and Katsura, we formulate and exactly solve a minimal two-term parent on any connected graph. Its fixed-number ground states have quartet off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) without charge-\(2e\) ODLRO, while an exact mapping to classical hard-core exclusion dynamics yields the full fixed-sector gap and a branch of quartet-density modes. Nonzero quartet stiffness and vanishing inverse quartet compressibility identify this \(z=2\) parent as a phase-separation boundary. Second, for a finite-range fermionic family with explicit quartet transfer and sufficiently large onsite penalty, we rigorously prove quartet ODLRO without charge-\(2e\) ODLRO at half quartet filling, both at the hypercubic XY point for \(d\geq2\) and throughout a finite XXZ interval on the square lattice. Third, we derive a strong-coupling realization using only electron hopping and two-body interactions. With local gap \(U_0\), pair hopping \(K\) generates quartet motion at order \(K^2/U_0\), whereas electron hopping \(t\) first contributes at order \(t^4/U_0^3\); charge-\(2e\) excitations remain gapped at \(O(U_0)\). On bipartite lattices, positive inverse quartet compressibility opens an asymptotically controlled homogeneous \(z=1\) regime with short-ranged pair correlations, while negative curvature drives phase separation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a rigorous framework for a direct charge-\(4e\) superconductor showing coherent four-electron (quartet) order without any charge-\(2e\) condensation, via an exactly solvable graph parent, a fermionic family with proven quartet ODLRO, and a strong-coupling realization from electron hopping and two-body interactions.
AI.motivation: Conventional superconductivity is built on charge-\(2e\) Cooper pairing, so the possibility of a direct charge-\(4e\) superconductor—where four-electron order condenses while every charge-\(2e\) channel stays uncondensed—is conceptually striking and poorly understood microscopically. The authors aim to establish minimal models and rigorous criteria for quartet off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO), to characterize its quantum phases, and to show it can arise from purely electronic ingredients.
AI.method: The work proceeds in three parts. (i) A minimal two-term parent Hamiltonian is formulated and exactly solved on any connected graph, building on \(\eta\)-clustering states and a bipartite parent; fixed-number ground states are analyzed, and an exact mapping to classical hard-core exclusion dynamics gives the fixed-sector gap and quartet-density modes. (ii) For a finite-range fermionic family with explicit quartet transfer and a large onsite penalty, quartet ODLRO without charge-\(2e\) ODLRO is rigorously proven at half quartet filling, at the hypercubic XY point for \(d\geq2\) and over a finite XXZ interval on the square lattice. (iii) A strong-coupling effective theory is derived from electron hopping \(t\), pair hopping \(K\), and local gap \(U_0\), with a perturbative bookkeeping of quartet versus pair processes.
AI.result: The exactly solvable parent exhibits quartet ODLRO without charge-\(2e\) ODLRO, with nonzero quartet stiffness and vanishing inverse quartet compressibility, identifying it as a phase-separation boundary of dynamical exponent \(z=2\). AI.conclusion: A direct charge-\(4e\) superconductor can be realized and controlled microscopically: quartet order can condense while charge-\(2e\) pairing stays uncondensed, the minimal parent sits at a phase-separation boundary, and strong-coupling electronic models support both a homogeneous \(z=1\) quartet phase and a phase-separated regime depending on the sign of the quartet compressibility.

title: Corbino-Enhanced Supersonic Acoustic-Emission Threshold in a GaAs Two-Dimensional Electron System
summary: We report nonlinear differential-resistance measurements in a high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron system patterned in a Corbino geometry. At zero magnetic field, $R_{\mathrm{diff}}(I_{dc})$ exhibits a pronounced polarity-selective threshold peak on the negative-current branch, gradually suppressed by a perpendicular magnetic field. We interpret the Corbino anomaly as a local Cherenkov-like threshold for acoustic phonon emission, enabled by the radial current concentration $j_r(r)=I/(2πr)$, which drives the local electron velocity above the sound velocity in a region adjacent to the inner contact. The polarity selectivity is attributed to Peltier heating and cooling, which modify the local thermal and boundary conditions near the contact, rather than to the kinematic threshold itself. Our results identify the Corbino geometry as a sensitive platform for probing local nonequilibrium electron--phonon processes in a high-mobility electron system within an independently established hydrodynamic-crossover regime and suggest that the inner Corbino contact can act as a geometry-defined source for supersonic acoustic emission.

AI.tldr: Nonlinear differential-resistance measurements in a Corbino-patterned GaAs/AlGaAs 2DES reveal a polarity-selective threshold peak at zero field, interpreted as a local Cherenkov-like threshold for acoustic phonon emission enabled by radial current concentration, with polarity selectivity arising from Peltier heating/cooling.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to probe local nonequilibrium electron–phonon processes in a high-mobility electron system and to exploit the Corbino geometry's radially concentrated current to access a hydrodynamic-crossover regime where local electron velocity can exceed the sound velocity.
AI.method: Nonlinear differential-resistance measurements, R_diff(I_dc), were performed on a high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron system patterned in a Corbino geometry, with a perpendicular magnetic field applied to test the field dependence of the anomaly.
AI.result: At zero magnetic field, R_diff(I_dc) shows a pronounced polarity-selective threshold peak on the negative-current branch, which is gradually suppressed by a perpendicular magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: The Corbino anomaly is interpreted as a local Cherenkov-like threshold for acoustic phonon emission driven by the radial current concentration j_r(r)=I/(2πr), which pushes the local electron velocity above the sound velocity near the inner contact. The polarity selectivity is attributed to Peltier heating and cooling modifying local thermal/boundary conditions rather than to the kinematic threshold. The Corbino geometry is identified as a sensitive platform for probing local nonequilibrium electron–phonon processes, and the inner contact can act as a geometry-defined source of supersonic acoustic emission.

title: Effective Mass Approach to Dynamics of Non-Markovian Systems with Short Memory
comment: Doctoral dissertation in a form of a guide through a collection of scientific articles (with minor corrections after the review). Written under the supervision of Jakub Spiechowicz. 53 pages, 12 figures + 1 logo
summary: Memory is an inherent feature of the dynamics of physical systems. It typically emerges when the complex structure of the system is simplified during the modeling process, obscuring a part of its underlying behavior. Consequently, the correct description of such a physical model requires knowledge of not only its present, but also its past states, leading to non-Markovian dynamics. The resulting interactions depending on the system history, however, introduce a significant layer of mathematical complexity. For this reason, when the memory time is significantly shorter than the time scales characterizing the dynamics, it is typically neglected at the cost of losing information regarding its role in the system behavior. In this dissertation, I introduce a novel methodology, namely the effective mass approach, which bridges the Markovian and non-Markovian regimes and provides an accessible framework for analyzing systems with short memory. In this method, the non-Markovian system is approximated with its Markovian counterpart, in which the short-memory effects are encapsulated within an effective mass. I then utilize this approach to demonstrate that the impact of short memory on physical dynamics can be remarkably pronounced. In particular, I show that the directed transport of a Brownian particle in an environment exhibiting temporal correlations can be reversed relative to its behavior in a memoryless medium. Moreover, I propose a setup wherein memory serves as a~control parameter for the generation of random information bits. Collectively, the results of this dissertation underscore the critical importance of short-time correlations in microscopic systems.

AI.tldr: The dissertation introduces the "effective mass approach," bridging Markovian and non-Markovian regimes by absorbing short-memory effects into an effective mass. Applying it reveals that short memory can reverse directed Brownian transport and can act as a control parameter for generating random information bits, underscoring the importance of short-time correlations.
AI.motivation: Memory (non-Markovian dynamics) is inherent to physical systems and arises when modeling simplifies a system's complex structure, obscuring part of its behavior. Correctly describing such systems requires past states, but history-dependent interactions introduce substantial mathematical complexity. Because of this, short memory (when memory time is much shorter than dynamical time scales) is typically neglected, at the cost of losing information about its role. A framework is needed that retains short-memory effects while remaining tractable.
AI.method: The "effective mass approach": the non-Markovian system is approximated by its Markovian counterpart, with short-memory effects encapsulated within an effective mass. This bridges the Markovian and non-Markovian regimes and provides an accessible framework for analyzing systems with short memory.
AI.result: The approach demonstrates that short memory can have a remarkably pronounced impact: (1) the directed transport of a Brownian particle in a temporally correlated environment can be reversed relative to its behavior in a memoryless medium; (2) a setup is proposed in which memory serves as a control parameter for generating random information bits.
AI.conclusion: Collectively, the results underscore the critical importance of short-time correlations in microscopic systems, showing that neglecting short memory can discard physically significant effects.

title: GRAINSMITH: A Generator of Polycrystalline Models for Atomistic Simulations with Statistical and Grain-Boundary Morphology Control
summary: Atomistic studies of grain-boundary engineering, grain-size effects and dopant enrichment require reproducible models with prescribed microstructural features. We present GRAINSMITH, an open-source Python package for generating statistically controlled polycrystalline models with selectable grain-boundary morphologies for molecular dynamics and subsequent relaxation. Within supported feature combinations, a single configuration specifies grain-size and volume distributions, crystallographic texture, boundary-area-weighted disorientation-angle distributions, phase composition and grain-boundary dopant placement. Crystal construction supports 230 crystallographic space groups. Periodic Voronoi and volume-targeted Laguerre tessellations provide planar boundaries, while distinct geometry backends generate smoothly curved and band-limited self-affine boundaries. A registry of twenty-six checks assesses applicable inputs, construction properties and outputs. Each run exports LAMMPS data and Extended XYZ files together with structural and statistical descriptors and machine-readable provenance. For a fixed software version and computational environment, the configuration and random seed determine byte-reproducible atomic configurations and scientific data across supported worker counts. By combining statistical specification, boundary-morphology control and reproducible atomistic output, GRAINSMITH supports systematic studies of microstructural effects and quantitative comparisons across generated models.

AI.motivation: Atomistic studies of grain-boundary engineering, grain-size effects, and dopant enrichment require reproducible models with prescribed microstructural features, which existing tools do not readily provide.
AI.method: A single configuration specifies grain-size and volume distributions, crystallographic texture, boundary-area-weighted disorientation-angle distributions, phase composition, and grain-boundary dopant placement. Crystal construction supports 230 crystallographic space groups. Periodic Voronoi and volume-targeted Laguerre tessellations produce planar boundaries, while distinct geometry backends generate smoothly curved and band-limited self-affine boundaries. A registry of twenty-six checks validates inputs, construction properties, and outputs.

title: Observation of Kondo Effect in Rhombohedral Graphene Superlattices
summary: Kondo effect in strongly correlated systems arises from the antiferromagnetic coupling between itinerant conduction electrons and localized magnetic moments, giving rise to a variety of exotic quantum phenomena. Two-dimensional moiré superlattice systems provide a highly tunable platform featuring topological flat bands, where Wannier orbitals are spatially confined by the periodic moiré potential and serve as localized magnetic moments, enabling the observable Kondo effect. Here we experimentally demonstrate Kondo interactions in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices through magneto-transport and temperature-dependent measurements. With increasing magnetic field, the magnetoresistance exhibits an increase-decrease transition across a critical field B_c, while the Hall resistance R_xy undergoes a sign reversal near B_c. Moreover, as temperature decreases, the longitudinal resistance R_xx first increases logarithmically and then decreases following a T^2 behavior, indicating a transition to heavy fermion liquid. These behaviors can be consistently explained by the breakdown of Kondo singlets induced by either magnetic field or temperature, which liberates carriers previously bound to localized moments, thereby enhancing conductivity and altering the dominant carrier type. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the Kondo interaction can be continuously tuned by both carrier density n and displacement electric field D, and suggest the emergence of a Kondo insulating state. Our findings provide deep insight into the Kondo effect in moiré engineered flat-band systems, paving the path for exploring exotic correlated quantum phases.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates Kondo interactions in hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices, evidenced by a field-driven magnetoresistance increase-decrease transition with Hall sign reversal and a temperature-driven crossover from logarithmic to T^2 behavior, all explained by the breakdown of Kondo singlets; the Kondo coupling is tunable by carrier density and displacement field, indicating a possible Kondo insulating state.
AI.motivation: The Kondo effect in strongly correlated systems, arising from antiferromagnetic coupling between itinerant conduction electrons and localized magnetic moments, hosts exotic quantum phenomena. Two-dimensional moiré superlattices offer a highly tunable platform with topological flat bands, where moiré-confined Wannier orbitals act as localized magnetic moments, providing an ideal venue to realize and study the Kondo effect.
AI.method: Magneto-transport and temperature-dependent measurements on hexalayer rhombohedral graphene moiré superlattices, including magnetoresistance, Hall resistance R_xy, and longitudinal resistance R_xx as functions of magnetic field and temperature, with additional tuning via carrier density n and displacement electric field D.
AI.result: With increasing magnetic field, magnetoresistance shows an increase-decrease transition across a critical field B_c, while R_xy reverses sign near B_c. As temperature decreases, R_xx first increases logarithmically and then decreases following T^2 behavior, signaling a transition to a heavy fermion liquid. The Kondo interaction is continuously tunable by carrier density and displacement field, and a Kondo insulating state is suggested.
AI.conclusion: The observed behaviors are consistently explained by the breakdown of Kondo singlets induced by magnetic field or temperature, which liberates carriers previously bound to localized moments, enhancing conductivity and altering the dominant carrier type. These findings provide deep insight into the Kondo effect in moiré engineered flat-band systems and pave the way for exploring exotic correlated quantum phases.

title: Avalanche Size and Interevent Time Statistics in Amorphous System
summary: The intermittent, stick-slip flow of amorphous systems is characterized by avalanches whose statistical properties display robust power-laws. In this paper, we study avalanche statistics in a field theoretical model of a soft-glassy system under shear. The order parameter in our model is the fluidity, which is related to the local rate of plastic events in a soft-glass. While avalanche sizes $S$ have been extensively characterized, the statistics of interevent times $t_i$ have remained largely unexplored. Here, we find that both $S$ and $t_i$ are power-law distributed and that their scaling exponents satisfy a precise relation. The model enables the analytical derivation of the scaling exponents and the reproduction of the behavior observed across a wide class of amorphous systems.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes avalanche statistics in a field-theoretical soft-glassy model under shear, showing that both avalanche sizes and interevent times follow power laws with exponents satisfying a precise relation.
AI.motivation: Avalanche sizes in amorphous systems have been well characterized, but the statistics of interevent times remain largely unexplored. The paper aims to fill this gap by studying both quantities and linking their scaling behavior.
AI.method: A field-theoretical model of a soft-glassy system under shear is used, with fluidity as the order parameter related to the local rate of plastic events. The model allows analytical derivation of the scaling exponents for avalanche sizes and interevent times.
AI.result: Both avalanche sizes S and interevent times t_i are found to be power-law distributed, and their scaling exponents satisfy a precise relation. The model analytically reproduces the behavior observed across a wide class of amorphous systems.
AI.conclusion: The field-theoretical approach provides an analytical explanation for the power-law statistics of avalanche sizes and interevent times, capturing universal behavior in amorphous systems.

title: Carrier-mediated spin helices in low-dimensional systems: Josephson-interference features and correlation renormalization
summary: Carrier-induced helical magnetism can arise in interacting one-dimensional systems coupled to localized moments. Here, we investigate the coupled-wire sliding-Luttinger-liquid counterparts with and without valley degrees of freedom, using isolated Tomonaga-Luttinger liquids as reference limits. The carrier spin susceptibility mediates a Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida interaction that selects the helical ordering wave vector, while interchannel correlations lock the relative helix phases and stabilize a collective quasi-two-dimensional texture. Using a variational treatment, we estimate the helix-induced partial gap and analyze the reconstruction of the remaining gapless carrier modes. To probe the spatial texture through transport, we incorporate the helix into an anisotropic superconductor-normal-metal-superconductor Josephson junction motivated by the coupled-channel structure of twisted bilayer WTe$_2$. We exploit flux focusing near the junction interfaces to make an applied in-plane field a controlled probe of the spin helix. Relative to junctions without the helix, the helical exchange field modifies the central-lobe width and relative lobe weights. In the transverse-channel geometry, it also produces field-dependent side-lobe asymmetry and central-peak displacement, which remain negligible in the matched references for the parameters considered. The reconstructed carrier sector also exhibits modified local-density-of-states exponents, spin-relaxation behavior, and competing correlations, with distinct signatures in isolated and coupled-wire systems. Our results connect collective helical order in coupled-wire systems to carrier-sector reconstruction and identify field-tunable Josephson interferometry as a complementary transport probe of the spatial spin texture.

This helix produces detectable signatures in Josephson interferometry (lobe widths, side-lobe asymmetry) and reconstructs the carrier sector, offering a transport probe of the spatial spin texture relevant to twisted bilayer WTe2.

The paper aims to connect collective helical order in coupled-wire systems to carrier-sector reconstruction and to identify a field-tunable transport probe of the spatial spin texture.

Carrier spin susceptibility mediates an RKKY interaction that selects the helical ordering wavevector, while interchannel correlations lock relative helix phases. In the transverse-channel geometry, it produces field-dependent side-lobe asymmetry and central-peak displacement, both negligible in matched reference systems for the parameters considered. title: Quantum-interference-driven orbital density wave and high-temperature superconductivity in trilayer nickelates
summary: Intertwined charge-density-wave (CDW) and spin-density-wave (SDW) orders are a hallmark of high-temperature superconducting multilayer nickelates. In trilayer La4Ni3O_{10}, charge correlations develop at temperatures above the onset of long-range spin order, and the characteristic ordering wavevectors satisfy $Q_{cdw} \approx 2Q_{sdw}$. Here, using a density-wave equation with vertex corrections, we show that quantum interference between short-range SDW fluctuations at $q \approx Q_{sdw}$ on the outer NiO2 layers generates an inter-outer-layer bond order at $Q_{cdw} \approx 2 Q_{sdw}$. This bond order induces a pronounced inner-layer-centered orbital order, with antiphase modulations of the Ni $d_{3z^2-r^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ occupations, producing strong orbital polarization but only weak total charge modulation. This intertwined bond-and-orbital order accounts for the layer-selective electronic reconstruction inferred from NMR/NQR and is consistent with Raman spectroscopy and scanning tunnelling microscopy measurements. The same orbital and spin fluctuations also cooperate to stabilize $s_{\pm}$-wave superconductivity through $M_z$ mirror-parity selection rules. Our results provide a unified microscopic framework for intertwined density-wave order and high-Tc superconductivity in multilayer nickelates.

AI.tldr: Quantum interference between short-range SDW fluctuations on the outer NiO2 layers of trilayer La4Ni3O10 generates an inter-outer-layer bond order at Qcdw ≈ 2Qsdw, which induces inner-layer-centered orbital order and, together with spin fluctuations, stabilizes s±-wave superconductivity via Mz mirror-parity selection rules.
AI.motivation: Intertwined CDW and SDW orders are a hallmark of high-Tc multilayer nickelates, and in trilayer La4Ni3O10 charge correlations appear above the onset of long-range spin order with Qcdw ≈ 2Qsdw. The microscopic origin of this intertwined order and its relationship to the layer-selective electronic reconstruction and to superconductivity remained unresolved.
AI.method: A density-wave equation with vertex corrections is used to study how short-range SDW fluctuations at q ≈ Qsdw on the outer NiO2 layers interfere quantum-mechanically, generating a bond order at Qcdw ≈ 2Qsdw, and to examine the resulting orbital order and its cooperation with spin fluctuations for pairing.
AI.result: Quantum interference between short-range SDW fluctuations on the outer layers produces an inter-outer-layer bond order at Qcdw ≈ 2Qsdw. This bond order induces a pronounced inner-layer-centered orbital order with antiphase modulations of Ni d3z2-r2 and dx2-y2 occupations, yielding strong orbital polarization but only weak total charge modulation. The intertwined bond-and-orbital order accounts for the layer-selective electronic reconstruction inferred from NMR/NQR and is consistent with Raman spectroscopy and scanning tunnelling microscopy. The same orbital and spin fluctuations cooperate to stabilize s±-wave superconductivity through Mz mirror-parity selection rules.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified microscopic framework for intertwined density-wave order and high-Tc superconductivity in multilayer nickelates, explaining the observed ordering wavevector relation, the weak charge but strong orbital modulation, and the layer-selective electronic reconstruction.

title: Modified Low-Temperature Scanning Tunneling Microscope for Ultrafast Pump-Probe Spectroscopy
summary: Combining scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with terahertz pulses (THz-STM) enables ultrafast dynamics of phonons, spins, and charge carriers to be probed with atomic-scale spatial and sub-picosecond temporal resolution. However, coupling THz radiation into a low-temperature STM junction presents some technical challenges as it requires optical access for laser illumination while maintaining junction stability. Instead of designing a completely new STM head with customized optical access and optics within the ultra-high vacuum chamber, we modified a Besocke "Beetle" style STM with minimal changes of the cryogenic radiation shields. Despite the given geometrical conditions, we achieved efficient coupling of THz and optical pulses to the STM junction while maintaining temperatures below 6 K. We designed the optical setup on a separate laser table, starting with femtosecond laser pulses that are used to generate THz pulses in a LiNbO$_3$ crystal. We show the obtained THz pulse shapes and determine the effective time resolution using cross-correlation measurements. We further demonstrate the stable performance of the modified STM by measuring THz-induced tunneling currents from monolayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS$_2$) grown on Au(111). The resulting current maps resolve atomic-scale contrast revealing a point defect. The measurements confirm efficient THz coupling and stable low-temperature STM operation with atomic resolution.

AI.tldr: The authors retrofit a Besocke "Beetle" STM with minimal cryogenic shield modifications to couple THz and optical pulses into a low-temperature junction, achieving sub-6 K operation and atomic-resolution THz-induced tunneling current maps of monolayer MoS₂ on Au(111).
AI.motivation: THz-STM enables ultrafast phonon, spin, and charge-carrier dynamics with atomic spatial and sub-picosecond temporal resolution, but coupling THz radiation into a low-temperature STM junction is technically challenging because it requires optical access for laser illumination while preserving junction stability. Rather than building a new STM head with customized optical access and in-vacuum optics, the authors seek a simpler route.
AI.method: A Besocke "Beetle"-style STM was modified with minimal changes to the cryogenic radiation shields. Femtosecond laser pulses on a separate laser table generate THz pulses in a LiNbO₃ crystal, and both THz and optical pulses are coupled to the STM junction. THz pulse shapes were characterized and effective time resolution determined via cross-correlation measurements. Performance was validated by measuring THz-induced tunneling currents from monolayer MoS₂ grown on Au(111).
AI.result: Efficient THz and optical pulse coupling to the STM junction was achieved while maintaining temperatures below 6 K. The obtained THz pulse shapes and effective time resolution were quantified by cross-correlation. THz-induced tunneling current maps from monolayer MoS₂ on Au(111) show atomic-scale contrast and resolve a point defect, confirming efficient THz coupling and stable low-temperature operation with atomic resolution.
AI.conclusion: A conventional Besocke "Beetle" STM can be adapted for THz-STM operation with only minimal cryogenic shield modifications, avoiding the need for a bespoke STM head and in-vacuum optics, while retaining sub-6 K stability and atomic resolution.

title: Stochastic optimisation method for estimating large deviations
summary: A stochastic optimisation method was recently proposed to efficiently compute large deviation functions, used in statistical physics to characterise the fluctuations of nonequilibrium systems, modelled as Markov processes. The method, called LDSTOP, combines numerical techniques from control theory and machine learning to iteratively construct the "driven process", a controlled version of the Markov process used as a model of nonequilibrium system that realises a given fluctuation or large deviation of that system in an optimal way. Compared to other methods based on spectral approximations, importance sampling, cloning or splitting, LDSTOP is simple, flexible, and scalable, as it works by simulating single trajectories that are gradually guided towards the driven process. Here, we illustrate these advantages by applying the method on the full range of Markov processes considered in applications, namely, discrete-time Markov chains, continuous-time jump processes, and diffusion processes. For each type, we define the objective function to be optimised, explain different options available for representing the driven process (using, e.g., neural networks), and provide implementation details through simple applications. With these contributions, we aim to showcase the method's efficiency, as well as its ease of use when combined with available machine learning packages, such as PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX, for simulating stochastic processes and solving high-dimensional optimisation problems.

AI.tldr: LDSTOP is a stochastic optimisation method that computes large deviation functions by iteratively constructing the driven process via single guided trajectories; this work illustrates its efficiency and flexibility across discrete-time chains, continuous-time jump processes, and diffusions.
AI.motivation: Large deviation functions characterize fluctuations of nonequilibrium systems modeled as Markov processes, but existing computational approaches—spectral approximations, importance sampling, cloning, or splitting—can be complex or hard to scale. LDSTOP was recently proposed as a simpler, flexible, scalable alternative, motivating a systematic demonstration of its applicability.
AI.method: LDSTOP combines numerical techniques from control theory and machine learning to iteratively construct the driven process—a controlled version of the Markov process realizing a given fluctuation or large deviation optimally. It works by simulating single trajectories gradually guided toward the driven process. The paper defines the objective function for discrete-time Markov chains, continuous-time jump processes, and diffusion processes, explains representation options for the driven process (e.g., neural networks), and provides implementation details through simple applications.
AI.result: The method is applied across the full range of Markov processes used in applications. For each type, the objective function is defined, representation options are explained, and implementation details are provided through simple applications, demonstrating efficiency and ease of integration with machine learning packages such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX.
AI.conclusion: LDSTOP showcases efficiency and ease of use for simulating stochastic processes and solving high-dimensional optimisation problems when combined with available machine learning packages, establishing practicality across diverse Markov process types.

title: Raman Scattering Evidence for Fluctuating Kagome-Plane Moments in $\mathrm{B} \parallel [111]$ in Pr$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ pyrochlore
summary: The exotic magnetic properties of the pyrochlore Pr$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ are determined by the coupling of spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom. Magnetism in this material originates from the non-Kramers Pr$^{3+}$ ion, and the exotic behavior has been discussed both in the framework of dipole-quadrupole properties of magnetic moments and disorder splitting the non-Kramers doublet. We use magneto-Raman spectroscopy to probe the crystal electric field (CEF) excitations of Pr$^{3+}$ in magnetic fields up to 14 T applied along the [100] and [111] crystallographic directions at 2 K. For $\mathrm{B}\parallel[100]$, the field evolution of the Raman active crystal field modes is quantitatively described by conventional Zeeman splitting of the Pr$^{3+}$ ground state doublet, including the thermally populated upper Zeeman branch at elevated temperature. For $\mathrm{}{B}\parallel[111]$, the spectra separate into responses from the triangular and kagome sublattices, and the CEF excitations of Pr$^{3+}$ on the triangular lattice exhibit the expected Zeeman shift consistent with full moments polarization. In contrast, the CEF excitations of Pr$^{3+}$ on the kagome lattice do not split as expected and instead broaden strongly with increasing field. This behavior is inconsistent with a static polarized configuration and is captured phenomenologically by a motional-narrowing description in which the kagome plane moments fluctuate between Zeeman-split levels on a meV timescale. This result offers a natural explanation for the reduced magnetization observed in $\mathrm{}{B}\parallel[111]$ and provides further evidence of the dipole-quadrupole properties of magnetic moments. It highlights Raman scattering as a sensitive probe of exotic spin-orbital dynamics in frustrated magnets.

AI.tldr: Magneto-Raman spectroscopy of Pr$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ reveals that for B$\parallel$[111], triangular-lattice Pr$^{3+}$ CEF excitations show normal Zeeman splitting/full moment polarization, while kagome-lattice excitations anomalously broaden without splitting, indicating meV-timescale moment fluctuations.
AI.motivation: The exotic magnetism of pyrochlore Pr$_2$Zr$_2$O$_7$ arises from coupled spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom of non-Kramers Pr$^{3+}$, and is debated between dipole-quadrupole moment frameworks and disorder-induced splitting of the non-Kramers doublet; a microscopic probe of the crystal electric field (CEF) excitations under field is needed.
AI.method: Magneto-Raman spectroscopy probing CEF excitations of Pr$^{3+}$ at 2 K in magnetic fields up to 14 T applied along the [100] and [111] crystallographic directions, analyzed via Zeeman splitting and a phenomenological motional-narrowing description.
AI.result: For B$\parallel$[100], the field evolution of Raman-active CEF modes is quantitatively described by conventional Zeeman splitting of the Pr$^{3+}$ ground-state doublet, including the thermally populated upper Zeeman branch at elevated temperature. For B$\parallel$[111], spectra separate into triangular and kagome sublattice responses: triangular-lattice Pr$^{3+}$ CEF excitations show the expected Zeeman shift consistent with full moment polarization, whereas kagome-lattice Pr$^{3+}$ CEF excitations do not split and instead broaden strongly with increasing field, inconsistent with a static polarized configuration and captured by motional narrowing with kagome-plane moments fluctuating between Zeeman-split levels on a meV timescale.
AI.conclusion: The anomalous kagome-lattice behavior offers a natural explanation for the reduced magnetization observed for B$\parallel$[111] and provides further evidence for the dipole-quadrupole properties of the magnetic moments, highlighting Raman scattering as a sensitive probe of exotic spin-orbital dynamics in frustrated magnets.

title: Photoresist-Free Lithography via Light-Induced Redox Patterning of Oxide Thin Films
summary: Lithographic patterning of nanoscale devices typically depends on photoresists, wet processing and multistep pattern-transfer workflows that impose both environmental and scaling constraints. Focused laser irradiation of (Ni,Co)1+2xTi1-xO3 under a reducing atmosphere drives localized oxygen removal, directly converting the insulating oxide into embedded metallic features without etching or chemical processing. Here we demonstrate a photoresist-free patterning method based on light-induced redox transformations in (Ni0.4Co0.6)3O3 (x = 1) thin films. Our results indicate that the transformation is self-limiting, as the high optical absorption of the emerging metallic phase restricts further energy penetration and confines the reduction front, producing conductive layers with electrical properties comparable to bulk metals. This reversible, orientation-preserving transformation is characteristic of a topotactic redox process, enabling direct nanoscale patterning without photoresists. The process is reversible through re-oxidation and is compatible with standard semiconductor wafer substrates. The role of Ti as a reduction inhibitor is discussed. These results establish a route to direct nanoscale patterning based on controlled redox chemistry, offering a potential alternative to conventional lithography for functional thin-film materials.

AI.tldr: A photoresist-free, direct nanoscale patterning method is demonstrated via light-induced, self-limiting topotactic redox transformation of (Ni0.4Co0.6)3O3 thin films, converting insulating oxide into embedded metallic features without etching or wet chemistry.
AI.motivation: Conventional lithographic patterning relies on photoresists, wet processing, and multistep pattern-transfer workflows, which impose environmental and scaling constraints. An alternative direct patterning route for functional thin-film materials is therefore desirable.
AI.method: Focused laser irradiation of (Ni,Co)1+2xTi1-xO3 under a reducing atmosphere drives localized oxygen removal. Using (Ni0.4Co0.6)3O3 (x = 1) thin films, light-induced redox transformation converts the insulating oxide into embedded metallic features without etching or chemical processing; the process is reversible via re-oxidation and compatible with standard semiconductor wafer substrates.
AI.result: The transformation is self-limiting because the high optical absorption of the emerging metallic phase restricts further energy penetration and confines the reduction front, yielding conductive layers with electrical properties comparable to bulk metals. The reversible, orientation-preserving transformation is characteristic of a topotactic redox process. The role of Ti as a reduction inhibitor is discussed.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a route to direct nanoscale patterning based on controlled redox chemistry, offering a potential alternative to conventional lithography for functional thin-film materials.

title: Lowest-known Energy Configuration of $N=100\,000$ Coulomb Charges in a Disk: Breaking the $10^{5}$ Barrier
comment: Article: 12 pages, 1 table; Supplemental Material: 6 pages, 6 figures, 1 table
summary: We report the first calculation of the lowest-known energy configuration for $N=100\,000$ classical point charges confined to a disk and interacting via the $1/r$ Coulomb potential - a system size never before achieved for the Thomson problem in a disk, more than doubling the previous record of $N=40\,886$ reported by Amore and Zarate. An adaptive defect-targeting subdomain optimization strategy yields an approximately linear growth of the wall-clock time per cycle with $N$; for $N=100\,000$ a single $24$-core CPU workstation without GPU acceleration required $\approx31$ hours. The energy $E_{\min}=7.80466624157\times10^{9}$ deviates from the asymptotic expansion fitted to $100\le N\le5000$ data by only $2.525\times10^{-7}$, providing a stringent test of its extrapolation to unprecedented scales. Bond-orientational order analysis reveals a polycrystalline bulk threaded by radial grain boundaries, establishing a new benchmark for two-dimensional Coulomb systems.

AI.tldr: The paper computes the lowest-known energy configuration for N=100,000 classical point charges confined to a disk interacting via the 1/r Coulomb potential (Thomson problem in a disk), more than doubling the previous record of N=40,886 by Amore and Zarate.
AI.motivation: Prior work on the Thomson problem in a disk was limited to system sizes up to N=40,886. Extending to much larger N provides a stringent test of the asymptotic energy expansion's extrapolation and establishes new benchmarks for two-dimensional Coulomb systems.
AI.method: An adaptive defect-targeting subdomain optimization strategy is employed. The approach achieves approximately linear growth of wall-clock time per cycle with N. For N=100,000, a single 24-core CPU workstation without GPU acceleration required about 31 hours.
AI.result: The energy E_min = 7.80466624157 x 10^9 deviates from the asymptotic expansion fitted to 100 <= N <= 5000 data by only 2.525 x 10^-7. Bond-orientational order analysis reveals a polycrystalline bulk threaded by radial grain boundaries.
AI.conclusion: The work sets a new record for the Thomson problem in a disk and establishes a new benchmark for two-dimensional Coulomb systems, while confirming the extrapolation validity of the asymptotic energy expansion at unprecedented scales.

title: III-V antiphase boundaries are not generated by Si or Ge substrate step edges
summary: We critically review recent experimental and theoretical advances on the valence- and structure-mismatched heteroepitaxy of III-V semiconductors on group-IV substrates. We examine key aspects including wetting behavior, atomic configurations at the hetero-interface, substrate passivation, and the stability of antiphase boundaries (APBs). By synthesizing these findings with pioneering studies, we propose a refined description of antiphase boundaries formation. Our analysis shows that hetero-interface formation is dictated by substrate terrace reconstruction, demonstrating that APBs are not generated at monoatomic step edges. This generalized III-V/IV growth framework provides new insights for the integration of III-V semiconductors on group-IV platforms and, more broadly, for valence-mismatched heteroepitaxy.

AI.tldr: This review synthesizes recent advances in III-V/group-IV heteroepitaxy, proposing a refined model of antiphase boundary (APB) formation governed by substrate terrace reconstruction rather than step edges.
AI.motivation: Valence- and structure-mismatched heteroepitaxy of III-V semiconductors on group-IV substrates is critical for integrating III-V functionality onto Si-based platforms, yet the mechanisms of hetero-interface formation and APB generation remain incompletely understood.
AI.method: A critical review and synthesis of recent experimental and theoretical studies, examining wetting behavior, atomic configurations at the hetero-interface, substrate passivation, and APB stability.
AI.result: Hetero-interface formation is dictated by substrate terrace reconstruction, and APBs are not generated at monoatomic step edges—contrary to earlier assumptions.
AI.conclusion: A refined, generalized III-V/IV growth framework is proposed, offering new insights for III-V-on-group-IV integration and for valence-mismatched heteroepitaxy broadly.

title: Model of the magnon Kerr effect in a highly anisotropic ferromagnet
summary: The magnon Kerr effect is a nonlinear phenomenon that occurs universally in any ferromagnet with finite magnetic anisotropy. It manifests itself as a magnon population-dependent change in the magnon dispersion relation. Here, we derive the Hamiltonian for the magnon Kerr effect for a thin film with uniaxial anisotropy. We consider the external field, parallel, perpendicular, and at an intermediate angle to the anisotropy axis, and determine the Kerr coefficient in each case. We show how the nonlinearity scales for different magnetic materials as a function of magnon frequency and magnetic sample volume. Moreover, we derive the equations of motion for a hybrid cavity-magnon system with such thin-film magnon Kerr nonlinearity, to obtain populations of photons and magnons, and scattering matrix terms for the microwave transmission of the cavity, relevant for experimental observations.

AI.tldr: This work derives the magnon Kerr Hamiltonian for thin films with uniaxial anisotropy under various field orientations, determines the Kerr coefficient and its scaling with magnon frequency, material, and sample volume, and formulates the equations of motion for a hybrid cavity-magnon system to obtain photon/magnon populations and microwave transmission scattering terms.
AI.motivation: The magnon Kerr effect is a universal nonlinear phenomenon in ferromagnets with finite magnetic anisotropy, manifesting as a magnon-population-dependent change in the magnon dispersion. A unified, orientation-dependent derivation of its Hamiltonian and coefficient for thin films is needed to understand and quantify this nonlinearity across different magnetic materials and geometries, and to connect it to experimentally observable cavity transmission.
AI.method: The authors derive the Hamiltonian for the magnon Kerr effect for a thin film with uniaxial anisotropy, considering an external field oriented parallel, perpendicular, and at an intermediate angle to the anisotropy axis, and determine the Kerr coefficient in each case. They analyze how the nonlinearity scales with magnon frequency, magnetic material, and sample volume. They then derive the equations of motion for a hybrid cavity-magnon system incorporating the thin-film magnon Kerr nonlinearity.
AI.result: A Kerr coefficient is obtained for each field orientation (parallel, perpendicular, intermediate) relative to the anisotropy axis. The nonlinearity scaling is characterized as a function of magnon frequency and magnetic sample volume across different magnetic materials. The equations of motion for the hybrid cavity-magnon system yield the photon and magnon populations and the scattering matrix terms for the microwave transmission of the cavity.
AI.conclusion: The magnon Kerr nonlinearity in uniaxial anisotropic thin films is systematically derived and quantified for arbitrary field orientations, with its scaling laws and its role in hybrid cavity-magnon systems characterized, providing the scattering-matrix expressions relevant for experimental microwave-transmission observations.

title: Infrared evidence for strong $C_{3}$ symmetry breaking in 1$T$-TiSe$_{2}$
summary: The interplay between lattice and electron degrees of freedom gives rise to competing ordered states in quantum materials, which can lead to a series of subsequent symmetry breaking transitions. While the differences are often subtle, these phases can be distinguished by their remaining point group symmetries. Here, we use infrared optical spectroscopy to probe symmetry breaking at the charge density wave transition of 1$T$-TiSe$_{2}$. We uncover a previously unobserved splitting of a doubly degenerate $E_u$ optical phonon at $T_{\mathrm{CDW}}\approx$ 190 K that constitutes direct evidence for the breaking of three-fold rotational symmetry. Our finding rules out proposals where the CDW transition to a low temperature chiral or nematic phase takes place through an intermediary state that preserves three-fold symmetry. The energy difference between the two former $E_{u}$ partners can only be explained by large $C_{3}$ breaking distortions of the same order of magnitude as previously observed changes in bond lengths, suggesting that $C_{3}$ symmetry breaking plays a dominant role in the CDW transition. The linewidth of the single phonon mode above $T_{\mathrm{CDW}}$ could be consistent with a fluctuating state where three-fold symmetry is also broken.

AI.tldr: Infrared spectroscopy of 1T-TiSe2 reveals a splitting of a doubly degenerate Eu optical phonon at the CDW transition (~190 K), providing direct evidence for C3 rotational symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: Competing ordered states in quantum materials arise from lattice-electron interplay and subsequent symmetry-breaking transitions; distinguishing these subtle phases requires probing their residual point group symmetries, which motivates a direct test of rotational symmetry breaking at the CDW transition in 1T-TiSe2.
AI.method: Infrared optical spectroscopy was used to probe symmetry breaking at the charge density wave transition of 1T-TiSe2, focusing on the behavior of a doubly degenerate Eu optical phonon across T_CDW.
AI.result: A previously unobserved splitting of the doubly degenerate Eu optical phonon at T_CDW ~ 190 K was found, constituting direct evidence for breaking of three-fold rotational symmetry. The energy difference between the former Eu partners implies large C3-breaking distortions comparable in magnitude to previously observed bond-length changes.
AI.conclusion: The findings rule out proposals in which the CDW transition to a low-temperature chiral or nematic phase proceeds via an intermediate state preserving three-fold symmetry, and indicate that C3 symmetry breaking plays a dominant role in the CDW transition. The linewidth of the single phonon mode above T_CDW may be consistent with a fluctuating state in which three-fold symmetry is also broken.

title: Device contacts as spin-state selectors for silicon vacancies in 4H-SiC
summary: Optically addressable defect spins in wide band gap semiconductors are promising building blocks for scalable quantum technologies. Yet, the consequences of conventional contact schemes used in semiconductor device integration for the quantum spin environment remain largely unexplored. Using the silicon vacancy (V$_\mathrm{Si}$) in silicon carbide (SiC) as a model system, we show that a widely used contact metal, nickel (Ni), intrinsically perturbs the defect spin state and quenches the characteristic emission from the spin-quartet channel of V$_\mathrm{Si}$. Low-energy muon spin rotation further reveals that Ni contacts create a magnetically contaminated region extending at least $\sim$120 nm into the SiC, in stark contrast to non-magnetic contacts such as Ti and Al. Moreover, cross-sectional cathodoluminescence measurements conducted on samples with box profiles of high defect density demonstrate a suppression of the quartet-state luminescence from the V$_\mathrm{Si}$ over a distance up to 500 nm beneath the Ni contact. This drastic influence on the defect's magnetic environment is accompanied by the appearance of a signature consistent with photoluminescence from the spin-doublet state of V$_\mathrm{Si}$ in the vicinity of the Ni layer, which was not observed in other material stacks. These results establish that even standard device configurations can drive quantum defects into unwanted charge and spin configurations, underscoring the necessity of precise design to preserve quantum-grade spin environments in semiconductor devices.

AI.tldr: Ni contacts used in SiC device integration intrinsically perturb and quench the silicon vacancy (V_Si) defect spin, creating a magnetically contaminated region extending hundreds of nanometers into the SiC and altering the defect's emission.
AI.motivation: Optically addressable defect spins in wide band gap semiconductors are promising for scalable quantum technologies, but the impact of conventional semiconductor-device contact schemes on the quantum spin environment remains largely unexplored. This gap motivated the study of how common contact metals affect defect spin coherence and emission.
AI.method: Using V_Si in SiC as a model system, the authors studied Ni contacts versus non-magnetic contacts (Ti, Al). They employed low-energy muon spin rotation to probe the magnetic environment and cross-sectional cathodoluminescence on samples with box profiles of high defect density to spatially map quartet-state luminescence near the contacts, also comparing other material stacks.
AI.result: Ni contacts intrinsically perturb the defect spin state and quench the characteristic emission from the spin-quartet channel of V_Si. Muon spin rotation revealed a magnetically contaminated region extending at least ~120 nm into the SiC, unlike Ti and Al. Cathodoluminescence showed suppression of quartet-state luminescence up to 500 nm beneath the Ni contact, accompanied by a signature consistent with photoluminescence from the V_Si spin-doublet state near the Ni layer, absent in other stacks.
AI.conclusion: Even standard device configurations can drive quantum defects into unwanted charge and spin configurations. Precise device design is necessary to preserve quantum-grade spin environments in semiconductor devices.

title: Collective Coordinate Dynamics of Antiferromagnet: Gravity by Quantum Metric
summary: The collective coordinate dynamics of antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic textures emerges as a geodesic equation governed by the quantum geometry of the CP$^1$ state associated with the Néel vector, rendering an effective Riemannian gravity and a Lorentz force in the texture motion. This unveils a physical scenario fundamentally distinct from the Thiele equation widely used for ferromagnetic textures, which is inertialess without any gravity analogy. Applying our framework to an optically driven ultrafast antiferromagnetic domain wall, we can explain the helicity-dependent asymmetric motion observed experimentally and predict a vibrantly breathing wall width.

AI.tldr: Antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic texture dynamics are reformulated as a geodesic equation derived from the quantum geometry of the CP$^1$ Néel-vector state, yielding effective Riemannian gravity and a Lorentz force—unlike the inertialess Thiele equation for ferromagnets. Applied to an optically driven ultrafast antiferromagnetic domain wall, the framework reproduces helicity-dependent asymmetric motion and predicts oscillatory wall-width breathing.
AI.motivation: The Thiele equation, the standard tool for ferromagnetic texture dynamics, is inertialess and lacks any gravity analogy, so it cannot capture the inertial, geometry-driven behavior expected for antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic textures. A framework is needed that accounts for the quantum geometry of the CP$^1$ Néel-vector state to describe their collective coordinate motion.
AI.method: The collective coordinate dynamics of antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic textures is derived as a geodesic equation governed by the quantum geometry of the CP$^1$ state associated with the Néel vector. This formulation gives rise to an effective Riemannian gravity and a Lorentz force in the texture motion. The framework is then applied to an optically driven ultrafast antiferromagnetic domain wall.
AI.result: The geodesic-equation description reveals effective Riemannian gravity and a Lorentz force acting in the texture motion, a scenario fundamentally distinct from the inertialess Thiele equation without gravity analogy. For the optically driven ultrafast antiferromagnetic domain wall, the framework explains the experimentally observed helicity-dependent asymmetric motion and predicts a vibrantly breathing wall width.
AI.conclusion: Antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic texture dynamics are governed by a geodesic equation rooted in the quantum geometry of the CP$^1$ Néel-vector state, producing effective Riemannian gravity and Lorentz-force effects absent in the ferromagnetic Thiele description. This framework accounts for helicity-dependent asymmetric domain-wall motion and predicts a breathing wall width, offering a new paradigm for ultrafast texture control.

title: Rapidly prototyping kagome flat band physics with acoustic metamaterials
summary: Flat bands with vanishing group velocity and quenched kinetic energy provide fertile ground for correlated states and exotic phenomena such as unconventional superconductivity. Yet, engineering and characterizing flat bands in quantum materials is time-consuming and costly, limiting the exploration of the vast design space of possible flat band systems. Acoustic metamaterials offer an accessible alternative: they can be easily simulated, cheaply fabricated, and quickly measured. Here we present a complete workflow to rapidly prototype flat band systems using acoustic metamaterials. Our design directly implements a tight-binding model using air cavities as lattice sites connected by channels that control hopping, allowing it to generalize to diverse lattice geometries. Using the kagome lattice as a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate excellent agreement between tight-binding theory, finite-element simulations, and experimental measurements. We then design a family of extended kagome lattices whose added sites cancel successively longer-range hopping, flattening the flat band. With fabrication and measurement requiring hours rather than months and a total cost orders of magnitude lower than quantum materials, our approach enables rapid iteration through candidate lattices, facilitating the discovery of new flat band physics in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a rapid-prototyping workflow for flat-band systems based on acoustic metamaterials, using air cavities and connecting channels to realize a tight-binding model. Demonstrated on kagome and extended kagome lattices, it achieves strong agreement among theory, finite-element simulation, and experiment at far lower cost and turnaround than quantum materials.
AI.motivation: Flat bands with vanishing group velocity and quenched kinetic energy host strongly correlated states and exotic phenomena, but engineering and characterizing them in quantum materials is slow and expensive, constraining exploration of the large flat-band design space. Acoustic metamaterials offer an accessible alternative that can be simulated, fabricated, and measured quickly and cheaply.
AI.method: A complete workflow is proposed to rapidly prototype flat-band systems using acoustic metamaterials. The design directly implements a tight-binding model in which air cavities act as lattice sites connected by channels that set the hopping amplitudes, allowing generalization to varied lattice geometries. The kagome lattice serves as proof-of-concept, validated by tight-binding theory, finite-element simulations, and experimental measurements. A family of extended kagome lattices is then designed, with added sites canceling successively longer-range hopping to flatten the flat band.
AI.result: Excellent agreement is found between tight-binding theory, finite-element simulations, and experimental measurements for the kagome lattice. The extended kagome designs progressively cancel longer-range hopping and flatten the flat band. Fabrication and measurement require hours rather than months, with total cost orders of magnitude lower than quantum materials.
AI.conclusion: The acoustic-metamaterial platform enables rapid iteration through candidate flat-band lattices, providing an efficient route to explore flat-band physics and facilitating the discovery of new correlated phenomena relevant to quantum materials.

title: From Local Atomic Motifs to Thermodynamic State: An Interpretable Physics-Informed Framework for Cu-Zr Metallic Glasses
summary: Machine-learning models that relate local atomic structure to the thermodynamic state of metallic glasses typically assess physical consistency after training rather than enforcing it during learning. Here, we develop a multi-task physics-informed neural network (PINN) that predicts temperature directly from Voronoi-motif population histograms while incorporating autograd-derived gradient constraints representing physically motivated relationships between structural motifs, quench rate, and temperature. The model simultaneously classifies each configuration as liquid, supercooled/transition, or glass through an auxiliary classification head. The classification task achieves 96.6% test accuracy with a macro-F1 score of 0.95, while the regression head yields a mean absolute error of 23.4 K on a trajectory-disjoint held-out test set. Five-fold trajectory-grouped cross-validation, deep-ensemble predictions, and Monte Carlo dropout are used to assess model robustness and predictive uncertainty. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate that physics constraints can be incorporated over a broad range of loss weights without compromising predictive accuracy, while substantially improving compliance with the prescribed physical trends. Benchmarking against conventional machine-learning regressors further demonstrates competitive predictive performance. SHAP analysis across the cross-validation ensemble identifies the coupled near-icosahedral motif family, particularly the full icosahedral motif and its single-atom-perturbed counterpart, as the dominant structural fingerprints of the glassy state. These results demonstrate that physically motivated constraints can be embedded directly into motif-based structure-property models, providing a pathway from post-hoc interpretability toward physically constrained machine learning for metallic glasses.

AI.tldr: A multi-task physics-informed neural network predicts temperature from Voronoi-motif histograms in metallic glasses while enforcing structural-physical gradient constraints and classifying liquid/supercooled/glass states.
AI.motivation: Existing machine-learning models linking local atomic structure to the thermodynamic state of metallic glasses assess physical consistency only after training. The authors aim to enforce physical relationships directly during learning, moving from post-hoc interpretability toward physically constrained ML.
AI.method: A multi-task physics-informed neural network (PINN) predicts temperature directly from Voronoi-motif population histograms, incorporating autograd-derived gradient constraints encoding relationships between structural motifs, quench rate, and temperature. An auxiliary classification head labels each configuration as liquid, supercooled/transition, or glass. Robustness and uncertainty are assessed via five-fold trajectory-grouped cross-validation, deep ensembles, and Monte Carlo dropout, with sensitivity analyses over physics-loss weights and benchmarking against conventional regressors. SHAP analysis is applied across the CV ensemble.
AI.result: The classification head reaches 96.6% test accuracy with a macro-F1 of 0.95, and the regression head yields a mean absolute error of 23.4 K on a trajectory-disjoint held-out test set. Physics constraints can be applied over a broad range of loss weights without sacrificing accuracy while substantially improving compliance with prescribed physical trends. SHAP identifies the coupled near-icosahedral motif family—especially the full icosahedral motif and its single-atom-perturbed counterpart—as the dominant structural fingerprints of the glassy state.
AI.conclusion: Physically motivated constraints can be embedded directly into motif-based structure-property models, offering a pathway from post-hoc interpretability toward physically constrained machine learning for metallic glasses.

title: Optimal probing scale for current fluctuations in a Brownian gyrator
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Code and data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22877097
summary: A driven colloidal rotor sustains a circulating current whose fluctuations one would like to bound. Any such bound rests on how strongly the current responds to a perturbation and on how much extra dissipation that perturbation costs, so there is a well-posed question of where to push: the response per unit Onsager-Machlup cost depends on the radius at which the probe acts, and is maximised at a definite one. We answer this for the Brownian gyrator and a quadrupolar shear under a Gaussian envelope, a probe chosen so that linear response is exactly blind to it at every observation window, so that the entire signal is second order. The problem separates: the cost is radial and does not see the circulation, while the response lives in the $m=3$ angular sector, where the resolvent reduces to Kummer's equation with $b=4$ and the susceptibility is a hypergeometric function of the envelope width. Maximising the ratio gives the optimal probing radius in closed form. It is set by whichever of the system's two clocks is faster: for weak driving $r^*=1.1264\sqrt{D/γ}$, the thermal radius of the trap, and for strong driving $r^*=1.5563\sqrt{D/Ω}$, the distance diffused in one radian of rotation, with the trap stiffness dropping out entirely. The crossover is at $Ω=γ$. Both limits, and the prefactors, are confirmed against direct simulation.

AI.tldr: Optimal probing radius for bounding fluctuations of a driven colloidal rotor current is derived in closed form, set by whichever of two system clocks is faster.
AI.motivation: To bound current fluctuations in a driven colloidal rotor, one needs to know how strongly the current responds to a perturbation versus how much extra dissipation that perturbation costs. Since the response per unit Onsager-Machlup cost depends on the probe radius, the open question is where to optimally apply the probe.
AI.method: Analyze the Brownian gyrator and a quadrupolar shear under a Gaussian envelope using a probe that is exactly invisible to linear response at every observation window, making the signal purely second order. The problem separates: cost is radial and independent of circulation, while response lies in the m=3 angular sector, where the resolvent reduces to Kummer's equation with b=4 and susceptibility becomes a hypergeometric function of the envelope width. The response-to-cost ratio is then maximized analytically.
AI.result: Optimal probing radius obtained in closed form, determined by the faster of two system clocks: for weak driving r* = 1.1264√(D/γ) (thermal trap radius), for strong driving r* = 1.5563√(D/Ω) (diffusion distance in one radian of rotation), with trap stiffness vanishing entirely. Crossover at Ω = γ. Both limits and prefactors confirmed by direct simulation.
AI.conclusion: The optimal probe radius for maximal response per unit dissipation cost is analytically determined and validated, revealing a clean crossover between thermal-trap-dominated and rotation-dominated regimes controlled by the ratio of rotation rate to damping rate.

title: Anisotropic Surface State Band Splitting and Low Energy Flat Bands in 3d Correlated Topological Kondo Insulator Candidate FeSb$_2$
summary: FeSb$_2$ is a correlated narrow-gap semiconductor that has often been discussed as a $3d$-electron Kondo insulator candidate and exhibits a low-temperature resistance plateau with possible surface-dominated conduction. We carried out a systematic high-resolution laser-based angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) study of FeSb$_2$ to investigate its electronic structure. The surface states around the zone center show clear anisotropic splitting. When the temperature is lowered into the resistance plateau regime ($<6\,\mathrm{K}$), the surface states remain robust, but their photoemission peaks become much sharper and gain spectral weight. Two distinct flat-band-like features are observed at low energy. One is located at $\sim$127 meV below the Fermi level, which exists only along a specific high-symmetry direction, while the other is located at $\sim$70 meV below the Fermi level and is present along all the measured momentum cuts around the zone center. These results provide new information to understand the renormalization effects, the resistance plateau, and the topological nature of FeSb$_2$.

AI.tldr: High-resolution laser ARPES on FeSb$_2$ reveals robust, anisotropically split surface states around the zone center, which sharpen and gain spectral weight upon cooling into the resistance plateau regime below 6 K, alongside two distinct low-energy flat-band-like features at ~127 meV and ~70 meV below $E_F$.
AI.motivation: FeSb$_2$ is a correlated narrow-gap semiconductor discussed as a $3d$-electron Kondo insulator candidate, exhibiting a low-temperature resistance plateau with possible surface-dominated conduction. Its electronic structure, renormalization effects, and topological nature remain unresolved, motivating a systematic high-resolution ARPES investigation.
AI.method: Systematic high-resolution laser-based angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) of FeSb$_2$, with temperature-dependent measurements performed down into the resistance plateau regime ($<6\,\mathrm{K}$), focusing on the electronic structure around the zone center.
AI.result: Surface states around the zone center show clear anisotropic splitting and remain robust upon cooling. Entering the resistance plateau regime ($<6\,\mathrm{K}$), their photoemission peaks become much sharper and gain spectral weight. Two distinct flat-band-like features appear at low energy: one at ~127 meV below the Fermi level, existing only along a specific high-symmetry direction, and another at ~70 meV below the Fermi level, present along all measured momentum cuts around the zone center.
AI.conclusion: The temperature-dependent surface-state behavior and the two flat-band-like features provide new information to understand the renormalization effects, the resistance plateau, and the topological nature of FeSb$_2$.

title: Perspective: The HSE Screened Hybrid and the Band Gap Problem: Origins, Impact, and the Contenders
summary: The ideas behind the screened hybrid functional HSE took shape in the early 2000s, about a quarter century ago. HSE was not explicitly designed to predict band gaps, although at the time we did recognize that hybrids could help address the band-gap problem. It was designed to make exact exchange affordable and physically defensible in extended systems. Keeping exact exchange at short range and screening it away at long range inverted the prescription developed for molecules. When HSE band gaps for ordinary semiconductors and selected metal oxides came out substantially closer to experiment than those obtained with conventional semilocal approximations, we were pleasantly surprised and encouraged by the path we had taken. The revision from HSE03 to HSE06 improved molecular thermochemistry while preserving the good accuracy for semiconductor gaps. The one-quarter exchange fraction was inherited unchanged from the successful unscreened PBE hybrid for molecules, rather than fitted to solids. HSE established a practical screened-hybrid approach for accurate band-gap calculations, expanding first-principles work in defect physics, photovoltaics, power electronics, and quantum information, among other areas. The first part of this Perspective recounts the decisions made at HSE's birth and their influence on subsequent developments. The second part assesses recent advances in semilocal and hybrid functionals against benchmarks on sets of solids. Recent meta-GGAs achieve HSE06-level accuracy for selected semiconductors, while dielectric-dependent and tuned hybrids address the limitations of fixed screening. These hybrid developments share with our early work on local hybrids and local range separation the aim of adapting exact exchange to the electronic environment. The comparisons assess band gaps alongside structures, energetics, computational cost, and transferability.

AI.tldr: A Perspective recounting the design decisions behind the HSE screened hybrid functional (~25 years on) and assessing recent semilocal and hybrid functional advances against solid-state benchmarks, especially for band gaps.
AI.motivation: HSE was not designed to predict band gaps but to make exact exchange affordable and physically defensible in extended systems. Its unexpected accuracy for semiconductor and metal-oxide gaps, plus the need to evaluate newer functionals against it, motivates this retrospective and assessment.
AI.method: Historical narrative of HSE's development (short-range exact exchange with long-range screening inverting the molecular prescription; HSE03-to-HSE06 revision; inherited one-quarter exchange fraction from PBE hybrids rather than fitting to solids), followed by benchmark comparisons of recent semilocal and hybrid functionals on sets of solids, examining band gaps alongside structures, energetics, computational cost, and transferability.
AI.result: HSE band gaps for ordinary semiconductors and selected metal oxides are substantially closer to experiment than conventional semilocal results; HSE06 preserved this gap accuracy while improving molecular thermochemistry. Recent meta-GGAs reach HSE06-level accuracy for selected semiconductors, and dielectric-dependent and tuned hybrids address the limitations of fixed screening.
AI.conclusion: HSE established a practical screened-hybrid approach for accurate band-gap calculations, enabling first-principles work in defect physics, photovoltaics, power electronics, and quantum information. Recent hybrid developments share with early local-hybrid and local-range-separation work the goal of adapting exact exchange to the electronic environment.

title: Navier-Stokes hydrodynamics near the critical point with out-of-equilibrium modes
summary: We investigate how slow out-of-equilibrium modes (OEM), introduced to extend the regime of validity of hydrodynamics near the critical point, fundamentally reshape the power spectrum of dynamical density fluctuations. We have used the equation of motion of slow modes for the situation when the extensive nature of thermodynamics is not altered due to the introduction of OEM. We find that the extensivity condition puts an extra constraint on the coupling of OEM with the four divergence of velocity. In the absence of OEM, the dynamic structure factor exhibits three Lorentzian peaks, one at zero frequency ($ω$), called Rayleigh peak and the other two called Brillouin peaks located symmetrically about $ω=0$. When the system is away from the critical point the inclusion of the OEM preserves the symmetry of the distributions but all the peaks acquire reduced widths and the Brillouin peaks adopt unequal heights. Irrespective of the value of OEM (zero or nonzero) the Brillouin peaks vanish near the critical point. The width of the Rayleigh peak substantially reduced in presence of OEM. Such reductions of the widths in presence of the OEM indicates the reduction in the decay rate of the fluctuation which leads to slowing down of decay of the fluctuations, a distinctive feature of the critical point.

AI.tldr: Introducing slow out-of-equilibrium modes (OEM) into hydrodynamic equations near a critical point narrows the Lorentzian peaks of the dynamic structure factor, indicating slower decay of density fluctuations, a hallmark of criticality.
AI.motivation: Standard hydrodynamics breaks down near the critical point, so slow out-of-equilibrium modes (OEM) were introduced to extend its regime of validity. This work asks how such OEM fundamentally reshape the power spectrum of dynamical density fluctuations.
AI.method: The authors use the equation of motion of the slow modes, assuming that the extensive nature of thermodynamics is preserved by the OEM. They impose an extensivity condition, which is shown to constrain the coupling of the OEM with the four-divergence of velocity, and then analyze the resulting dynamic structure factor.
AI.result: The extensivity condition imposes an extra constraint on the coupling between OEM and the four-divergence of velocity. Without OEM, the dynamic structure factor has three Lorentzian peaks: a Rayleigh peak at ω=0 and symmetric Brillouin peaks at ±ω.
