Away from criticality, OEM preserves the symmetry but reduces all peak widths and makes the Brillouin peaks unequal in height. Regardless of OEM value, Brillouin peaks vanish near the critical point, and the Rayleigh peak width is substantially reduced.
AI.conclusion: The narrowing of all Lorentzian peaks caused by OEM reflects a reduced decay rate of fluctuations, i.e., slowing down of fluctuation decay, which is the distinctive signature of the critical point.

title: Trade-off between interface morphology and compositional homogeneity in AlGaAs/GaAs quantum wells revealed by multislice electron ptychography
summary: AlGaAs/GaAs asymmetric coupled quantum wells (ACQWs) are promising platforms for enhanced second-order optical nonlinearities, with their performance strongly influenced by the structural quality of heterostructures. Flat interfaces, together with high compositional homogeneity, are generally desirable for optimizing device functionality. Here we show that sharp and flat AlGaAs/GaAs interface morphology dominates the second harmonic generation (SHG) response in AlGaAs/GaAs ACQWs, even when significant compositional fluctuations in Al/Ga occupancy are present within the AlGaAs layers. Using multislice electron ptychography, we resolve the three-dimensional (3D) interface morphology and compositional distribution in AlGaAs/GaAs ACQWs under distinct growth interruptions. Longer growth interruptions sharpen and flatten the AlGaAs/GaAs interfaces, but at the same time cause stronger compositional fluctuations in the AlGaAs layers. These findings clarify how growth interruption tunes quantum wells structures and provide direct guidance for quantum wells design in next-generation optoelectronic devices.

AI.tldr: Sharp, flat AlGaAs/GaAs interface morphology dominates the second harmonic generation response in asymmetric coupled quantum wells, even when significant Al/Ga compositional fluctuations exist within the AlGaAs layers, as revealed by multislice electron ptychography.
AI.motivation: AlGaAs/GaAs asymmetric coupled quantum wells (ACQWs) are promising for enhanced second-order optical nonlinearities, and their performance strongly depends on heterostructure structural quality. Flat interfaces and high compositional homogeneity are generally considered desirable, but the relative importance of interface morphology versus compositional uniformity for the second harmonic generation (SHG) response was unclear.
AI.method: The authors used multislice electron ptychography to resolve the three-dimensional interface morphology and compositional distribution in AlGaAs/GaAs ACQWs grown under different growth interruption conditions, and correlated these structural features with the SHG response.
AI.result: Sharp and flat AlGaAs/GaAs interface morphology was found to dominate the SHG response, even in the presence of significant compositional fluctuations in Al/Ga occupancy within the AlGaAs layers. Longer growth interruptions sharpened and flattened the interfaces but simultaneously induced stronger compositional fluctuations in the AlGaAs layers.
AI.conclusion: Interface morphology, rather than compositional homogeneity, is the dominant factor governing SHG in AlGaAs/GaAs ACQWs. These findings clarify how growth interruption tunes quantum well structures and offer direct guidance for quantum well design in next-generation optoelectronic devices.

title: Channel concentration of critical quantum geometry
comment: 44 pages, 7 figures (including Supplemental Material); code and data available at https://github.com/ToelUl/channel-concentration/tree/companion-2026-09-21-rc1
summary: The quantum metric quantifies the total ground-state response along a parameter direction, but does not resolve how excitations share that response. We define channel concentration (CC) as the sum of squared normalized response weights over specified excitation channels, such as momentum blocks. An exact finite-size theorem yields thermodynamic CCs of 2/3 for the field response of the critical transverse-field Ising model and 1/3 for the half-filled XX pairing response, despite the same leading metric scaling. In finite-size approaches to the XY Lifshitz point, field and anisotropy perturbations yield different concentrations despite a common limiting Hamiltonian with quadratic dispersion. In a unitary 1+1-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) on a circle, we consider a nondegenerate vacuum in a fixed sector perturbed by one spatially integrated scalar primary. We derive complete zero-momentum energy-level response weights, including descendants. For scaling dimension $0<Δ<3/2$, these weights determine the normalized response distribution and an exact universal concentration function. The expression reproduces the exact Ising lattice limit 2/3 and gives approximately 0.8515 for the three-state Potts thermal field, compared with approximately 0.800 from an exponent-only approximation. Finite-size interacting calculations compare concentrations and ranked response weights over many-body energy levels. These exact benchmarks show which response distinctions total metric scaling misses and guide comparisons with finite-size interacting spectra.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "channel concentration" (CC), a measure of how excitations share the ground-state response to a parameter perturbation, and derives exact thermodynamic and finite-size results—notably CC = 2/3 for the critical transverse-field Ising field response and 1/3 for the half-filled XX pairing response—plus a universal CFT-based concentration function for a scalar primary perturbation.
AI.motivation: The quantum metric quantifies the total ground-state response along a parameter direction but does not resolve how that response is distributed among different excitation channels (e.g., momentum blocks). The authors aim to capture this channel-resolved structure, since total metric scaling can be identical even when the underlying response distributions differ—as in the Ising versus XX cases and the field versus anisotropy perturbations near the XY Lifshitz point.
AI.method: They define channel concentration (CC) as the sum of squared normalized response weights over specified excitation channels, such as momentum blocks. An exact finite-size theorem is used to obtain thermodynamic CCs for the critical transverse-field Ising field response and the half-filled XX pairing response. Finite-size approaches are applied to the XY Lifshitz point to compare field and anisotropy perturbations. In a unitary 1+1-dimensional CFT on a circle, they consider a nondegenerate vacuum in a fixed sector perturbed by one spatially integrated scalar primary and derive complete zero-momentum energy-level response weights, including descendants. Finite-size interacting calculations are performed to compare concentrations and ranked response weights across many-body energy levels.
AI.result: Exact finite-size theorem yields thermodynamic CCs of 2/3 for the critical transverse-field Ising field response and 1/3 for the half-filled XX pairing response, despite identical leading metric scaling. Near the XY Lifshitz point, field and anisotropy perturbations produce different concentrations even though they share a limiting Hamiltonian with quadratic dispersion. For the CFT with scaling dimension 0 < Δ < 3/2, the derived response weights determine a normalized response distribution and an exact universal concentration function; this reproduces the exact Ising lattice limit 2/3 and gives approximately 0.8515 for the three-state Potts thermal field, versus approximately 0.800 from an exponent-only approximation. Finite-size interacting calculations compare concentrations and ranked response weights over many-body energy levels.
AI.conclusion: Channel concentration resolves response distinctions that total metric scaling misses, providing exact benchmarks that reveal which distinctions are invisible to metric scaling and guiding comparisons with finite-size interacting spectra.

title: Staged emergence of anomalous Hall transport in a correlated uranium Weyl semimetal
summary: Understanding how electronic correlations reshape topological states remains a central challenge in quantum materials. Here we investigate the uranium ferromagnet UPS using magnetotransport, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, thermodynamic measurements, and first principles calculations. Resonant photoemission reveals narrow U-$5f$ spectral weight at the Fermi level coexisting with broad incoherent states, consistent with the itinerant/localized duality characteristic of uranium $5f$ electrons. The anomalous Hall conductivity reaches approximately $4.5\times10^{2}\,Ω^{-1}\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$, yet does not simply follow the ordered magnetic moment. Temperature dependent photoemission reveals relatively little change across $T_C=118$~K, followed by a pronounced redistribution of low-energy $5f$ spectral weight below approximately 90~K. First-principles calculations identify a symmetry protected Weyl crossing with pronounced Berry curvature and yield an intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity of approximately $9.6\times10^{2}\,Ω^{-1}\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$. These results demonstrate that magnetic order, correlated electronic reconstruction, and anomalous Hall transport develop over distinct but overlapping temperature ranges, revealing how strong correlations reshape topological transport in a uranium Weyl semimetal.

AI.tldr: This study shows that in the uranium ferromagnet UPS, magnetic order, correlated 5f electronic reconstruction, and anomalous Hall transport emerge over distinct but overlapping temperature ranges, revealing how strong electronic correlations reshape topological transport in a uranium Weyl semimetal.
AI.motivation: Understanding how electronic correlations reshape topological states is a central challenge in quantum materials, particularly in uranium systems where 5f electrons exhibit itinerant/localized duality.
AI.method: The authors combined magnetotransport, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), thermodynamic measurements, and first-principles calculations on the uranium ferromagnet UPS.
AI.result: Resonant photoemission revealed narrow U-5f spectral weight at the Fermi level coexisting with broad incoherent states; anomalous Hall conductivity reached ~4.5×10² Ω⁻¹cm⁻¹ but did not simply track the ordered magnetic moment; temperature-dependent photoemission showed little change across T_C=118 K, with pronounced redistribution of low-energy 5f weight below ~90 K; first-principles calculations identified a symmetry-protected Weyl crossing with pronounced Berry curvature and an intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity of ~9.6×10² Ω⁻¹cm⁻¹.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic order, correlated electronic reconstruction, and anomalous Hall transport develop over distinct but overlapping temperature ranges, demonstrating how strong correlations reshape topological transport in a uranium Weyl semimetal.

title: Ultralow-Barrier Ion Transport in the Subnitride Electride Ba$_3$N for High-Rate Sodium Storage
summary: Electrides, ionic crystals in which excess electrons are delocalized within interstitial voids rather than bound to specific atomic sites, exhibit exotic physicochemical behaviors, yet their potential as electrochemical energy-storage hosts remains largely unexplored. Here, using comprehensive first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that the quasi-one-dimensional subnitride electride Ba$_3$N offers a compelling route to overcome the long-standing performance trade-offs in sodium-ion battery anodes. Spontaneous Na intercalation into the open interchain channels establishes thermodynamically stable phases, generating an exceptionally flat low-potential plateau that avoids the high-potential sloping losses of hard carbon while preserving an essential safety margin against dendrite formation. Crucially, the itinerant interstitial anionic electron sea dynamically flattens the potential landscape by suppressing site-specific orbital interactions, enabling ultrafast Na ion transport with an exceptionally low migration barrier. This work establishes a design paradigm for harnessing electride chemistry to achieve ultrafast battery electrodes.

AI.tldr: Using first-principles calculations, this work shows that the quasi-1D subnitride electride Ba3N is a promising sodium-ion battery anode: spontaneous Na intercalation into open interchain channels yields a flat low-potential plateau with a safe margin against dendrites, while the itinerant interstitial anionic electron sea flattens the potential landscape and enables ultrafast Na transport with a very low migration barrier, establishing an electride-chemistry design paradigm for ultrafast electrodes.
AI.motivation: Electrides—ionic crystals with excess electrons delocalized in interstitial voids—exhibit exotic physicochemical behaviors, but their potential as electrochemical energy-storage hosts remains largely unexplored. Meanwhile, sodium-ion battery anodes face long-standing performance trade-offs.
AI.method: Comprehensive first-principles calculations are used to evaluate the quasi-one-dimensional subnitride electride Ba3N as a sodium-ion battery anode host, examining Na intercalation into the open interchain channels, thermodynamic stability of the resulting phases, the potential profile, and Na ion migration barriers.
AI.result: Spontaneous Na intercalation into the open interchain channels establishes thermodynamically stable phases and produces an exceptionally flat low-potential plateau, avoiding the high-potential sloping losses of hard carbon while retaining a safety margin against dendrite formation. The itinerant interstitial anionic electron sea dynamically flattens the potential landscape by suppressing site-specific orbital interactions, yielding ultrafast Na ion transport with an exceptionally low migration barrier.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a design paradigm for harnessing electride chemistry to achieve ultrafast battery electrodes.

title: Quantum Mpemba effect from Stark localization
summary: In classical systems, rugged potential energy landscapes provide a transparent mechanism for the celebrated Mpemba effect, in which hotter initial states cool down faster. This picture generally does not survive in quantum systems. Here we show how to design a quantum energy landscape with local dissipation leading to an Mpemba effect with parametrically separated timescales. Our approach uses Stark localization to design an energy landscape and localized incoherent hopping as cooling mechanism. The hops are triggered by rare "detection" events whose rate grows with energy, allowing hotter states to cool faster and producing super-exponentially separated cooling rates for localized initial states. We further show that the effect is dramatically enhanced by collective hopping of bound pairs in the presence of attractive on-site interactions. These findings have clear experimental signatures accessible in present-day setups.

AI.tldr: The paper designs a quantum energy landscape via Stark localization, where localized incoherent hopping triggered by rare energy-dependent detection events yields an Mpemba effect with parametrically—even super-exponentially—separated cooling timescales, further amplified by collective hopping of attractive bound pairs.
AI.motivation: The classical mechanism for the Mpemba effect—rugged potential energy landscapes—generally fails to carry over to quantum systems. The authors aim to identify a genuinely quantum design principle that reproduces the effect with well-separated timescales.
AI.method: They engineer a quantum energy landscape using Stark localization and employ localized incoherent hopping as the cooling mechanism. Hops are activated by rare "detection" events whose rate increases with energy. Attractive on-site interactions are introduced to enable collective hopping of bound pairs.
AI.result: Hotter states cool faster, and localized initial states exhibit super-exponentially separated cooling rates. The Mpemba effect is dramatically enhanced by the collective hopping of bound pairs under attractive interactions. The findings yield clear experimental signatures accessible in current setups.
AI.conclusion: A quantum energy landscape built from Stark localization combined with energy-dependent detection-triggered hopping realizes a strong Mpemba effect with parametrically separated timescales, offering experimentally testable predictions in present-day platforms.

title: Sapphire-Side hBN Formation by Ni--Cr-Mediated Growth in a Stacked Ni--Cr/Boron/Sapphire Configuration: Effect of Boron Supply
summary: Metal-mediated growth provides an effective route to high-quality hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), but hBN formation on the metal does not necessarily ensure hBN formation on an adjoining dielectric substrate. Here, we investigate this distinction using a vertically stacked Ni--Cr/boron/sapphire configuration operated at 1550~$^\circ$C under atmospheric pressure, with the relative boron supply varied at fixed Ni:Cr = 8:2. hBN is detected by Raman spectroscopy on the gas-exposed alloy surface throughout the investigated Alloy:B range, whereas sapphire-side hBN appears only at the higher relative boron supplies of Alloy:B = 24:1 and 18:1, as confirmed by both Raman spectroscopy and XRD. The hBN (002) reflection further narrows as the boron supply increases from 24:1 to 18:1, corresponding to an increase in the apparent c-axis coherent length from approximately 86 to 143~nm. Additional crystalline reflections also emerge only under these higher-boron conditions. These results identify boron supply as a key parameter governing the transition from alloy-side hBN formation to concurrent sapphire-side hBN growth. Once formed, sapphire-side hBN occurs within a substantially reconstructed and chemically modified Al/O-rich sapphire environment rather than as a uniform film on an intact substrate. To our knowledge, this study provides the first demonstration of successful sapphire-side hBN formation by Ni--Cr-mediated growth.

AI.tldr: Ni–Cr-mediated growth at 1550 °C shows that alloy-surface hBN forms across all boron supplies, but sapphire-side hBN forms only at high relative boron (Alloy:B = 24:1 and 18:1), establishing boron supply as the key control parameter.
AI.motivation: Metal-mediated growth yields high-quality hBN, yet hBN formation on the metal does not guarantee formation on an adjoining dielectric substrate. This distinction—and the parameters controlling it—remains poorly understood, motivating a systematic study of the alloy-to-sapphire transition.
AI.method: A vertically stacked Ni–Cr/boron/sapphire configuration was operated at 1550 °C under atmospheric pressure, with Ni:Cr fixed at 8:2 and relative boron supply (Alloy:B) varied. Products were characterized by Raman spectroscopy and XRD to compare gas-exposed alloy-side and sapphire-side hBN.
AI.result: Alloy-side hBN was detected by Raman across the entire Alloy:B range. Sapphire-side hBN appeared only at Alloy:B = 24:1 and 18:1 (Raman and XRD). The hBN (002) reflection narrowed with increasing boron supply from 24:1 to 18:1, with apparent c-axis coherent length rising from ~86 to 143 nm. Additional crystalline reflections also emerged only under higher-boron conditions.
AI.conclusion: Boron supply governs the transition from alloy-side hBN formation to concurrent sapphire-side growth. Sapphire-side hBN forms within a substantially reconstructed, chemically modified Al/O-rich sapphire environment rather than as a uniform film on an intact substrate. This is the first demonstration of sapphire-side hBN formation by Ni–Cr-mediated growth.

title: Enhanced thermal conductivity of (010) (AlxGa1-x)2O3 epitaxial films utilizing indium-catalyzed molecular beam epitaxy
summary: (AlxGa1-x)2O3/beta-Ga2O3 transistors are an emerging candidate for high-power and high-frequency electronic devices. beta-Ga2O3 in particular is notably limited for anisotropic low thermal conductivity, which is further reduced in (AlxGa1-x)2O3 due to alloy and other defect-driven phonon scattering mechanisms. In this work we show that the thermal conductivity of (010) oriented (AlxGa1-x)2O3 thin films for 0.01 < x < 0.20, measured using time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR), is limited by alloy scattering without observable adverse scattering by additional defects. This is enabled through the synthesis of the (AlxGa1-x)2O3 films using molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) on \b{eta}-Ga2O3 substrates, leveraging indium-catalyzed growth to suppress dislocation formation and phase separation to achieve single-phase pseudomorphic films up to x = 0.2. This growth process improved the thermal conductivity of (AlxGa1-x)2O3 by 2X as compared to previously reported values. For increasing Al composition (x), we observe a steady decline in (AlxGa1-x)2O3 thermal conductivity due to alloy scattering which is validated using virtual crystal approximation (VCA) model. We also show that the thermal boundary conductance across the Al/(AlxGa1-x)2O3 interface is reduced with increasing x, which we posit is due to the stiffening of the (AlxGa1-x)2O3 acoustic modes with increasing x by comparing experimental results with a diffuse mismatch model (DMM). Overall, these thermal characteristics provide valuable insights for designing heterostructures with optimized interfaces and composition.

AI.tldr: Indium-catalyzed MBE grown (AlxGa1-x)2O3 thin films on β-Ga2O3 show 2× higher thermal conductivity than previous reports, with alloy scattering (not defects) limiting thermal transport, and reduced Al-interface thermal boundary conductance with increasing Al content.
AI.motivation: (AlxGa1-x)2O3/β-Ga2O3 transistors are promising for high-power and high-frequency electronics, but β-Ga2O3 suffers from anisotropic low thermal conductivity, further degraded in (AlxGa1-x)2O3 by alloy and defect-driven phonon scattering. Understanding and improving thermal transport in these alloys is essential for device design.
AI.method: (010)-oriented (AlxGa1-x)2O3 thin films (0.01 < x < 0.20) were synthesized by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) on β-Ga2O3 substrates using indium-catalyzed growth to suppress dislocation formation and phase separation, yielding single-phase pseudomorphic films up to x = 0.2. Thermal conductivity was measured by time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR), interpreted via the virtual crystal approximation (VCA) model, and interface thermal boundary conductance was compared to a diffuse mismatch model (DMM).
AI.result: Indium-catalyzed growth improved (AlxGa1-x)2O3 thermal conductivity by 2× versus prior reports. Thermal conductivity is limited by alloy scattering with no observable adverse defect scattering, and declines steadily with increasing Al composition (x), as validated by the VCA model. Thermal boundary conductance across the Al/(AlxGa1-x)2O3 interface decreases with increasing x, attributed to stiffening of (AlxGa1-x)2O3 acoustic modes, supported by DMM comparison.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that indium-catalyzed MBE enables high-quality pseudomorphic (AlxGa1-x)2O3 films with substantially improved thermal conductivity, where alloy scattering governs thermal transport and acoustic-mode stiffening reduces interface conductance. These findings offer valuable guidance for designing heterostructures with optimized interfaces and composition.

title: Deterministic control of antiferromagnetic domain walls by circular phonons
summary: In an antiferromagnet, areas with different orientations of the antiferromagnetic Néel vector, which plays the role of the order parameter, can coexist, thus forming antiferromagnetic domains separated by domain walls. This suggests that antiferromagnets can possess the functionalities of magnetic storage media. Whether one can benefit from these functionalities crucially depends on the availability of efficient means for deterministic control of antiferromagnetic domain walls. Here, we demonstrate an approach to deterministically control domain walls in the van der Waals antiferromagnet Ni-doped $MnPS_3$ via dynamic engineering of the crystal lattice. By resonantly exciting a pair of nearly degenerate orthogonal infrared-active $A_u$ and $B_u$ phonon modes with circularly polarized mid-infrared light, we induce helicity-dependent reconfiguration of 180° antiferromagnetic domains, providing evidence for a phonon-induced effective field conjugate to the Néel order parameter. The domain kinetics exhibit a pronounced helicity asymmetry governed by the interplay between domain-wall elasticity and defect-mediated pinning, enabling small phonon-driven perturbations to accumulate into stable domain transformations. Our results establish dynamic lattice control and defect engineering as means for deterministic control of antiferromagnetic order.

AI.tldr: By resonantly exciting nearly degenerate orthogonal infrared-active A_u and B_u phonon modes with circularly polarized mid-infrared light in the van der Waals antiferromagnet Ni-doped MnPS3, the authors achieve helicity-dependent reconfiguration of 180° antiferromagnetic domains, evidencing a phonon-induced effective field conjugate to the Néel order parameter.
AI.motivation: Antiferromagnets can host domains of differing Néel vector orientations separated by domain walls, suggesting potential use as magnetic storage media. Realizing this functionality requires efficient, deterministic means to control antiferromagnetic domain walls, which remains a key challenge.
AI.method: Dynamic crystal lattice engineering in the van der Waals antiferromagnet Ni-doped MnPS3. A pair of nearly degenerate, orthogonal infrared-active A_u and B_u phonon modes is resonantly excited using circularly polarized mid-infrared light, inducing helicity-dependent reconfiguration of 180° antiferromagnetic domains. Domain kinetics are analyzed in terms of the interplay between domain-wall elasticity and defect-mediated pinning.
AI.result: Helicity-dependent reconfiguration of 180° antiferromagnetic domains is observed, providing evidence for a phonon-induced effective field conjugate to the Néel order parameter. The domain kinetics show a pronounced helicity asymmetry, governed by the interplay between domain-wall elasticity and defect-mediated pinning, which allows small phonon-driven perturbations to accumulate into stable domain transformations.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic lattice control combined with defect engineering offers a viable route for deterministic control of antiferromagnetic order, advancing the prospect of antiferromagnet-based storage functionalities.

title: Dual Role of Mobile Interstitials in Defect Kinetics: From Retardation to Acceleration
summary: Mobile interstitial atoms redistribute while defects migrate, complicating prediction of defect kinetics and leading to contradictory reports of acceleration and retardation. We formulate defect activation in a grand-canonical ensemble at fixed interstitial chemical potential and define a pathway free-energy landscape $ΔG(Λ;T,μ)$ and the corresponding activation free energy $ΔG^{\ddagger}$. We compute these quantities using both hyperplane-constrained thermodynamic integration via a mean force relation and a two-state chemical-potential integration, denoted TSCPI. The latter requires sampling only the initial and transition states; a single chemical-potential integration then yields $ΔG^{\ddagger}(T,μ)$ across a wide $μ$ range, enabling rapid mapping over temperature and chemical potential. Applied to vacancy diffusion in FCC, BCC, and HCP metals with H (including in plane and cross plane diffusion in Zr) and in BCC W with He, both free energy routes agree with diffusion coefficients from molecular dynamics mean square displacements. The resulting maps reveal regimes of suppression and enhancement, including a crossover from suppression to enhancement with increasing hydrogen concentration. A site occupancy analysis links barrier shifts to state dependent site spectrum changes and transferable interstitial interaction terms.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates defect activation in a grand-canonical ensemble at fixed interstitial chemical potential, defining a pathway free-energy landscape and activation free energy computed via two independent methods, validated against MD diffusion coefficients and revealing suppression/enhancement regimes.
AI.motivation: Mobile interstitial atoms redistribute as defects migrate, complicating prediction of defect kinetics and producing contradictory reports of both acceleration and retardation. A framework is needed to consistently capture how a variable interstitial population (fixed chemical potential) reshapes defect migration barriers and rates.
AI.method: Defect activation is cast in a grand-canonical ensemble at fixed interstitial chemical potential, defining a pathway free-energy landscape ΔG(Λ;T,μ) and activation free energy ΔG‡. Two routes are used: (1) hyperplane-constrained thermodynamic integration via a mean force relation, and (2) a two-state chemical-potential integration (TSCPI) requiring sampling only initial and transition states, with a single chemical-potential integration yielding ΔG‡(T,μ) over a wide μ range for rapid temperature/chemical-potential mapping.
AI.result: Applied to vacancy diffusion in FCC, BCC, and HCP metals with H (including in-plane and cross-plane diffusion in Zr) and in BCC W with He, both free-energy routes agree with diffusion coefficients obtained from molecular dynamics mean square displacements. The resulting maps reveal regimes of suppression and enhancement, including a crossover from suppression to enhancement with increasing hydrogen concentration. A site occupancy analysis links barrier shifts to state-dependent site spectrum changes and transferable interstitial interaction terms.
AI.conclusion: The grand-canonical free-energy framework and its two computational routes provide a consistent, rapid means to predict how interstitial chemical potential and temperature tune defect migration, resolving conflicting acceleration/retardation observations and offering transferable insight via site occupancy and interstitial interaction terms.

title: Revealing tilt-driven structural heterogeneity in hybrid improper ferroelectrics by spatially-resolved crystallography
summary: Domain walls in ferroic oxides can host emergent functionalities that differ fundamentally from those of the surrounding bulk, making their microscopic structure central to understanding and controlling macroscopic behaviour. We use scanning three-dimensional X-ray diffraction to map the spatial evolution of coupled octahedral distortion modes across ferroelastic domain walls in the hybrid improper ferroelectric Ca$_{2.15}$Sr$_{0.85}$Ti$_{2}$O$_{7}$. By combining tomographic reconstruction with symmetry-adapted analysis of the octahedral rotation and tilt and associated strain modes, we map their spatial evolution across individual walls in the bulk crystal. We find that the walls are intrinsically extended, with widths far exceeding those expected for conventional Ising-like ferroic interfaces. The wall structure is characterised by a continuous rotation of the tilt order parameter through a tetragonal intermediate. These results provide new microscopic insight into the structural mechanisms governing ferroelastic wall formation, ferroelectric switching, and emergent functionality at domain walls.

AI.tldr: Using scanning 3D X-ray diffraction and symmetry-adapted analysis, the authors map octahedral distortion and strain modes across ferroelastic domain walls in Ca2.15Sr0.85Ti2O7, revealing intrinsically extended walls with a continuous tilt-order-parameter rotation through a tetragonal intermediate.
AI.motivation: Domain walls in ferroic oxides host emergent functionalities distinct from the bulk, so their microscopic structure is key to understanding and controlling macroscopic behaviour. Existing knowledge of the internal structure of ferroelastic walls in hybrid improper ferroelectrics remains limited.
AI.method: Scanning three-dimensional X-ray diffraction combined with tomographic reconstruction and symmetry-adapted analysis of octahedral rotation, tilt, and associated strain modes to map their spatial evolution across individual domain walls in bulk Ca2.15Sr0.85Ti2O7.
AI.result: The walls are intrinsically extended, with widths far exceeding those expected for conventional Ising-like ferroic interfaces, and their structure features a continuous rotation of the tilt order parameter through a tetragonal intermediate.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide new microscopic insight into the structural mechanisms governing ferroelastic wall formation, ferroelectric switching, and emergent functionality at domain walls.

title: Phase field modelling of microstructure transformations in Zr-Sn alloy during irradiation
summary: In this work we study peculiarities of spatial rearrangement of solute and vacancy concentrations in Zr-Sn alloy at stages of both thermal treatment of solid solution and irradiation of annealed alloy under reactor conditions. To this end, we exploit phase field modelling including reaction rate theory and CALPHAD method combined in one generalized approach. Simulations were done in 3D in order to get a detailed information about rearrangement of solutes and defects in a bulk. We discuss the emergence of the secondary phase at the stage of thermal treatment and its stability under neutron irradiation. We analyze an influence of the irradiation dose onto statistical properties of the secondary phase particles.

AI.tldr: This work models the spatial redistribution of Sn solute and vacancy concentrations in Zr-Sn alloy during thermal treatment and reactor irradiation, using a unified 3D phase-field, reaction-rate-theory, and CALPHAD framework. It examines secondary-phase precipitation, its stability under neutron irradiation, and the dose dependence of precipitate statistics.
AI.motivation: Understanding how solute and vacancy concentrations rearrange in Zr-Sn alloys during thermal processing and under irradiation is important for predicting microstructural evolution and secondary-phase behavior in reactor-relevant conditions, which single-method models cannot fully capture.
AI.method: A generalized phase-field modelling approach integrating reaction rate theory and the CALPHAD method. Simulations are performed in 3D to resolve solute and defect rearrangement in the bulk, covering both thermal treatment of the solid solution and irradiation of the annealed alloy under reactor conditions.
AI.result: The study captures the emergence of the secondary phase during thermal treatment and evaluates its stability under neutron irradiation. It further analyzes how irradiation dose affects the statistical properties of secondary-phase particles.
AI.conclusion: The combined phase-field/CALPHAD/reaction-rate framework provides a consistent means to describe coupled solute-vacancy rearrangement and secondary-phase evolution in Zr-Sn alloys, linking thermal-treatment precipitation to its irradiation-induced stability and dose-dependent characteristics.

title: Tailoring structural, electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of rare-earth gallates RGaO$_3$ (R = Ho, Er, Tm) via first-principles investigations
summary: Ab initio calculations of cubic perovskites RGaO$_3$ (R = Ho, Er, Tm) were performed using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave (FP-LAPW) method within the framework of density functional theory (DFT). We investigated their structural, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties in detail. In the optimized configurations, the lattice constants ranged from 3.83 to 3.85 A. The electronic band structures indicate that ErGaO$_3$ is semiconducting, whereas HoGaO$_3$ and TmGaO$_3$ exhibit half-metallic behavior, probably due to the interaction of spin-orbit coupling with the electronic states near the Fermi level. Optical response of half-metallic compounds (HoGaO$_3$,TmGaO$_3$) is strongly governed by their spin polarization electronic structure. The semiconducting spin channel absorbs ultraviolet photons, while metallic or small gap channel interacts with infrared light. This dual behavior enables spin selective optical excitation, relevant for spintronics and optoelectronics applications. These compounds show high surface reflectivity, with TmGaO$_3$ achieving a maximum reflectivity of 69%. Moreover, their optical conductivity mainly occurs at higher energies, indicating suitability for high-energy optoelectronic applications. The calculated magnetic moments suggest a robust ferromagnetic character across this series.

AI.tldr: DFT FP-LAPW study of cubic RGaO3 (R = Ho, Er, Tm): lattice constants 3.83-3.85 Å; ErGaO3 is semiconducting while HoGaO3 and TmGaO3 are half-metallic, enabling spin-selective optical excitation relevant to spintronics/optoelectronics.
AI.motivation: The rare-earth gallate perovskites RGaO3 (R = Ho, Er, Tm) are of interest for spintronics and optoelectronics, yet a systematic ab initio characterization of their structural, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties across this series is needed to clarify how spin polarization governs their functional response.
AI.method: Full-potential linearized augmented plane wave (FP-LAPW) calculations within density functional theory (DFT) were performed on cubic perovskites RGaO3 (R = Ho, Er, Tm). Structural optimization yielded the lattice constants, and the electronic band structures, magnetic moments, and optical response (reflectivity and optical conductivity) were computed, including the role of spin-orbit coupling near the Fermi level.
AI.result: Optimized lattice constants span 3.83-3.85 Å. ErGaO3 is semiconducting, whereas HoGaO3 and TmGaO3 exhibit half-metallic behavior, likely due to spin-orbit coupling interaction with states near the Fermi level. Optical response of the half-metallic compounds is strongly governed by their spin-polarized electronic structure: the semiconducting spin channel absorbs ultraviolet photons while the metallic/small-gap channel interacts with infrared light, giving dual, spin-selective optical excitation. High surface reflectivity is found, with TmGaO3 reaching a maximum of 69%, and optical conductivity occurs mainly at higher energies. Calculated magnetic moments indicate robust ferromagnetic character across the series.
AI.conclusion: Cubic RGaO3 (R = Ho, Er, Tm) display robust ferromagnetism and tunable electronic character (half-metallic for HoGaO3 and TmGaO3, semiconducting for ErGaO3). Their spin-selective, dual-channel optical response and high-energy optical conductivity make them promising candidates for spintronics and high-energy optoelectronic applications.

title: Computational investigation of a perovskite LaBiO$_{3}$ for photovoltaic, thermoelectric, and optoelectronic applications
summary: Using density functional theory (DFT) with the ONCVVPSP pseudopotential and PBE functional, this study investigates the structural, electronic, elastic, optical, and thermoelectric properties of the trigonal LaBiO$_{3}$ perovskite oxide (space group R3c). Ground-state parameters lattice constant, volume, bulk modulus, and its pressure derivative were determined using the equation of state. Applying the Hubbard correction (GGA+U) revealed an indirect, wide band gap of 3.51 eV. Mechanical properties, including the anisotropy factor, elastic modulus, and Poisson's ratio, were calculated via the Voigt-Reuss-Hill averaging scheme. The bulk-to-shear modulus ratio identifies the trigonal phase as ductile. Additionally, Debye temperatures and sound velocities were computed. Optical characteristics (absorption coefficient, refractive index, and electron energy loss function) were evaluated across a 0-35 eV spectral range. Finally, semi-classical transport coefficients, including electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and power factor, were calculated to assess the material's thermoelectric potential.

AI.tldr: DFT (ONCVVPSP, PBE) with GGA+U reveals trigonal LaBiO3 (R3c) as an indirect 3.51 eV band-gap oxide with ductile mechanical behavior, characterized across structural, elastic, optical, and thermoelectric properties.
AI.motivation: The study aims to characterize the largely unexplored trigonal LaBiO3 perovskite oxide, providing first-principles data on its structural, electronic, elastic, optical, and thermoelectric behavior to assess its functional potential.
AI.method: Density functional theory with ONCVVPSP pseudopotentials and the PBE functional; ground-state parameters via equation of state; GGA+U (Hubbard correction) for the band structure; elastic constants analyzed through the Voigt-Reuss-Hill averaging scheme, including anisotropy factor, elastic moduli, Poisson's ratio, Debye temperature, and sound velocities; optical response computed over 0-35 eV; semi-classical transport coefficients evaluated for thermoelectric performance.
AI.result: Ground-state lattice constant, volume, bulk modulus, and its pressure derivative were obtained. GGA+U yields an indirect wide band gap of 3.51 eV. The bulk-to-shear modulus ratio indicates ductility. Debye temperatures and sound velocities were determined. Absorption coefficient, refractive index, and electron energy loss function were evaluated from 0-35 eV. Electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and power factor were calculated for thermoelectric assessment.
AI.conclusion: Trigonal LaBiO3 (R3c) is a wide-band-gap, mechanically ductile perovskite oxide whose optical and thermoelectric coefficients are quantified, establishing a baseline for its potential optoelectronic and thermoelectric applications.

title: Electronic energy structure and optical properties of In$_{4}$CdI$_{6}$ from $\textit{ab initio}$ calculations
summary: This work presents the $\textit{ab initio}$ calculations of the electronic energy spectrum of the In$_{4}$CdI$_{6}$ compound. The study was conducted within the framework of density functional theory (DFT), using local density approximation (LDA) and general gradient approximation (GGA) pseudopotentials, and the Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) hybrid functional. The GGA approximation was implemented using the PBE and PBEsol exchange-correlation functional. Based on the electronic energy structure, the type of the minimum band gap was determined, and an analysis of the energy level dispersion for both the valence and conduction bands was performed. Furthermore, the effective masses of electrons ($\textit{m}_{c}$) and holes ($\textit{m}_{v}$) for In$_{4}$CdI$_{6}$ were established. The energy band analysis was complemented by the calculation of the density of states (DOS). Based on the electronic energy spectrum, the real and imaginary components of the dielectric function are calculated. Using the Kramers-Kronig relations, we also derive such fundamental optical functions of In$_{4}$CdI$_{6}$ as the refractive index $\textit{n}$, and the extinction coefficient $\textit{k}$.

AI.tldr: This work reports ab initio DFT calculations (LDA, GGA-PBE/PBEsol, and HSE06) of the electronic energy spectrum of In4CdI6, determining the band gap type, band dispersion, effective masses of electrons and holes, density of states, and the dielectric function with derived optical functions (refractive index n, extinction coefficient k) via the Kramers-Kronig relations.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to establish the electronic energy spectrum and related optical properties of the In4CdI6 compound, which appear to be lacking a detailed ab initio characterization.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using LDA and GGA pseudopotentials (GGA implemented with PBE and PBEsol exchange-correlation functionals) as well as the HSE06 hybrid functional. From the computed electronic energy structure, the minimum band gap type and valence/conduction band dispersion were analyzed, effective electron (mc) and hole (mv) masses were determined, and the density of states (DOS) was computed. The real and imaginary parts of the dielectric function were then calculated, and the refractive index n and extinction coefficient k were derived using the Kramers-Kronig relations.
AI.result: The type of the minimum band gap was determined, energy level dispersion for the valence and conduction bands was analyzed, effective masses of electrons (mc) and holes (mv) were established, the DOS was calculated, and the real/imaginary dielectric function components along with the refractive index n and extinction coefficient k were derived.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a comprehensive ab initio characterization of the electronic and optical properties of In4CdI6, yielding band structure parameters (gap type, dispersion, effective masses, DOS) and fundamental optical functions (dielectric function, n, k).

title: A small-distortion geometric model for elasto-plasticity in single crystals driven by the motion of dislocations
summary: A central problem in nonlinear elasto-plasticity theory is to formulate a geometrically nonlinear, large-strain model of elasto-plasticity in single crystals in which plastic flow is driven directly by the motion of dislocations and which allows for a homogenization procedure from discrete dislocation lines to dislocation densities. In this work, such a model is introduced based on two hypotheses: (1) The Small-Distortion Hypothesis posits that the total plastic distortion may be arbitrarily large but its dominant part admits a representation as a gradient, meaning that the distorting effect of dislocations is small relative to the specimen size. Concretely, this hypothesis is realized here through a "multiplicative Helmholtz-type decomposition", which splits an arbitrary matrix field into the product of a gradient and a matrix field with controlled curl. (2) The Line-Tension Approximation treats all dislocations as infinitesimally thin lines whose local stress fields are individually negligible compared to specimen-scale stresses and only matter in the aggregate. The resulting model, termed the Small-Distortion Geometric Model, furthermore employs the so-called Space-Time Framework, which furnishes a geometric language to precisely describe the advection of dislocation lines. As such, it provides a physically grounded account of crystal plasticity in an idealized mesoscopic setting that bridges dislocation mechanics and continuum elasto-plasticity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Small-Distortion Geometric Model, a geometrically nonlinear, large-strain single-crystal elasto-plasticity model driven directly by dislocation motion and amenable to homogenization from discrete dislocation lines to dislocation densities.
AI.motivation: Formulating a geometrically nonlinear, large-strain model of single-crystal elasto-plasticity in which plastic flow is driven directly by dislocation motion and which permits homogenization from discrete dislocation lines to dislocation densities remains a central open problem.
AI.method: The model rests on two hypotheses: (1) the Small-Distortion Hypothesis, stating that the total plastic distortion may be arbitrarily large but its dominant part admits a gradient representation (distortion induced by dislocations is small relative to specimen size), realized via a multiplicative Helmholtz-type decomposition splitting an arbitrary matrix field into a gradient times a matrix field with controlled curl; and (2) the Line-Tension Approximation, treating dislocations as infinitesimally thin lines whose individual local stress fields are negligible relative to specimen-scale stresses and matter only in aggregate. The construction further employs the Space-Time Framework to describe the advection of dislocation lines.
AI.result: The outcome is the Small-Distortion Geometric Model, which provides a geometric language for precisely describing dislocation-line advection and constitutes a physically grounded account of crystal plasticity in an idealized mesoscopic setting.
AI.conclusion: The model bridges dislocation mechanics and continuum elasto-plasticity by enabling homogenization from discrete dislocation lines to dislocation densities within a geometrically nonlinear, large-strain framework.

title: Ultrahigh Thermal Conductivity in Isotopically Ultrapure Single-Crystal Diamond
summary: Diamond has the highest thermal conductivity among natural materials. Reducing isotope scattering can further push the limit of thermal conductivity of diamond. Here, we report the room-temperature thermal conductivity of a diamond single crystal with an exceptionally low ppm-level 13C content. Secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) reveals a 13C concentration of only ~0.00024% and negligible other impurities, placing this sample as the most isotopically purified diamond samples reported to date. Time-domain thermoreflectance measurements show a room-temperature thermal conductivity of ~3100 W m-1 K-1. Although this value is markedly higher than that of natural diamond, it remains comparable to the best reported values for less isotopically 12C pure diamond. This result suggests that additional phonon-scattering mechanisms beyond isotope scattering may exist at this extreme isotopic purification level. Vacancy defects may contribute to the remaining suppression of thermal conductivity.

AI.tldr: A diamond single crystal with ultra-low 13C content (~0.00024%) achieves a room-temperature thermal conductivity of ~3100 W m-1 K-1, the isotopic purity being the highest reported, yet the value remains comparable to less isotopically pure diamond, suggesting other phonon-scattering mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Diamond has the highest thermal conductivity among natural materials, and reducing isotope scattering is expected to further raise this limit. However, it is unclear how far isotopic purification alone can push thermal conductivity, motivating a test at the extreme low-13C limit.
AI.method: Secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) was used to quantify 13C concentration and impurities, yielding ~0.00024% 13C and negligible other impurities. Time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) was employed to measure room-temperature thermal conductivity.
AI.result: The sample is the most isotopically purified diamond reported to date. Its room-temperature thermal conductivity is ~3100 W m-1 K-1, markedly higher than natural diamond but comparable to the best values reported for less isotopically 12C-pure diamond.
AI.conclusion: At this extreme isotopic purification level, phonon-scattering mechanisms beyond isotope scattering appear to persist. Vacancy defects may account for the remaining suppression of thermal conductivity.

title: Electronic-Entropy-Driven Phase Transitions in Compressed Iron Oxides
summary: Electronic entropy is usually treated as a secondary correction to structural stability, but under strong electronic excitation it can become a primary thermodynamic driving force. Here we show that electronic entropy can drive both polymorphic and stoichiometric phase transformations in compressed iron oxides. Using finite-temperature density functional theory, we calculate the electronic-temperature-dependent Gibbs free energies of Fe$_2$O, FeO, Fe$_4$O$_5$, Fe$_3$O$_4$, and multiple Fe$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs, including $α$-, $ι$-, $ζ$-, $η$-, and $θ$-Fe$_2$O$_3$, over the pressure range 60--260 GPa. At 60-140 GPa, electronic excitation mainly reorganizes the relative stability of Fe$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs, driving transitions from $ι$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ to $η$-Fe$_2$O$_3$. At 180 GPa, the free-energy landscape becomes strongly competitive as FeO is stabilized over an intermediate range of electronic temperature, while $η$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ becomes favourable at higher T. At 220-260 GPa, the lowest-free-energy phase at low T is the Fe-rich compound Fe$_2$O, but increasing electronic temperature stabilizes FeO. These results demonstrate that electronic entropy can control not only the relative stability of crystal structures at fixed composition, but also the competition between different iron-oxide stoichiometries. The predicted electronic-entropy-driven phase boundaries provide a route to nonthermal structural transformations in ultrafast and high-energy-density experiments.

AI.tldr: Electronic entropy, typically a minor correction in structural stability, is shown via finite-temperature DFT to act as a primary thermodynamic driver of polymorphic and stoichiometric phase transitions in compressed iron oxides (Fe2O, FeO, Fe4O5, Fe3O4, and several Fe2O3 polymorphs) across 60-260 GPa.
AI.motivation: Electronic entropy is conventionally regarded as only a secondary correction to structural stability, yet under strong electronic excitation it can become a dominant thermodynamic force. The authors aim to demonstrate that electronic entropy can govern not only polymorphic stability at fixed composition but also competition among different stoichiometries, providing a mechanism for nonthermal transformations relevant to ultrafast and high-energy-density experiments.
AI.method: Finite-temperature density functional theory (DFT) is used to compute electronic-temperature-dependent Gibbs free energies of Fe2O, FeO, Fe4O5, Fe3O4, and multiple Fe2O3 polymorphs (alpha-, iota-, zeta-, eta-, and theta-Fe2O3) over the pressure range 60-260 GPa.
AI.result: At 60-140 GPa, electronic excitation mainly reorganizes the relative stability of Fe2O3 polymorphs, driving iota- to eta-Fe2O3 transitions. At 180 GPa, the free-energy landscape becomes strongly competitive: FeO is stabilized over an intermediate electronic-temperature range, while eta-Fe2O3 is favored at higher T. At 220-260 GPa, the lowest-free-energy phase at low T is the Fe-rich compound Fe2O, but increasing electronic temperature stabilizes FeO.
AI.conclusion: Electronic entropy can control both the relative stability of crystal structures at fixed composition and the competition between different iron-oxide stoichiometries. The predicted electronic-entropy-driven phase boundaries offer a route to nonthermal structural transformations in ultrafast and high-energy-density experiments.

title: Small-supercell and Small-dataset Training Strategy of Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Point Defects
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can treat large-scale material systems with near first-principles accuracy and have been widely used to accelerate point-defect simulations. However, the training of MLIPs usually relies on large amounts of DFT data. This issue is particularly pronounced for charged defects, for which DFT calculations of large supercells are required to avoid long-range Coulomb interactions and finite-size effects, making the construction of datasets computationally expensive. In this work, we propose an efficient MLIP training scheme for neutral and lowly charged point defects based on small supercells (less than 100 atoms) and limited number of DFT calculations. The scheme requires only four DFT structural relaxations to construct the training dataset and the trained MLIPs dedicated for the defect can predict the defect formation energies in larger supercells (over 200 atoms) with small errors (mostly smaller than 0.3 eV). Using defects in GaN, SiO$_2$, and $\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{ZnSnS}_4$ as representative examples, we evaluate the extrapolation capability of this scheme for predicting defect total energies and structural relaxations across different supercell sizes. The results show that an MLIP trained only on single small defect supercell produces severe errors when treating large supercells. Incorporating defect data from multiple supercell sizes improves the predictive performance of the MLIP, while adding pristine defect-free bulk supercells further enhances the accuracy. These results provide practical guidance for training MLIP models of defect systems with low computational costs.

AI.tldr: A cost-efficient MLIP training scheme using small supercells (<100 atoms) and only four DFT relaxations predicts defect formation energies in large supercells (>200 atoms) with errors mostly below 0.3 eV, with accuracy improved by combining data from multiple supercell sizes and pristine bulk.
AI.motivation: Training MLIPs for point defects normally requires large amounts of DFT data, and for charged defects large supercells are needed to avoid long-range Coulomb interactions and finite-size effects, making dataset construction computationally expensive.
AI.method: Propose an efficient MLIP training scheme for neutral and lowly charged point defects based on small supercells (<100 atoms) and limited DFT calculations, requiring only four DFT structural relaxations to build the training set. Extrapolation capability is evaluated using defects in GaN, SiO2, and Cu2ZnSnS4 across different supercell sizes, testing training on single small supercells, multiple supercell sizes, and adding pristine bulk supercells.
AI.result: Trained defect-specific MLIPs predict formation energies in supercells over 200 atoms with small errors, mostly below 0.3 eV. An MLIP trained only on a single small defect supercell produces severe errors for large supercells; incorporating data from multiple supercell sizes improves performance, and adding pristine defect-free bulk supercells further enhances accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The scheme provides practical guidance for training MLIP models of defect systems at low computational cost, and multi-size defect data plus pristine bulk data are key to improving extrapolation to large supercells.

title: Vacancy aggregation enhances NV- spin coherence in diamond: a cluster-correlation-expansion study of multi-vacancy spin baths in semiconductors
summary: Annealing a semiconductor makes its vacancies mobile; they aggregate into multi-vacancy complexes that often carry spin. Such centres are a magnetic-noise source for any spin qubit among them, in silicon and silicon carbide as well as in diamond, and they are accordingly blamed for NV- decoherence in irradiated and implanted diamond, with two coherence records credited to removing them. Cluster-correlation-expansion simulations driven by published electron-paramagnetic-resonance parameters invert that attribution. At a fixed paramagnetic spin density a multi-vacancy bath gives a Hahn-echo coherence time 2.7-4.4 times longer than a bath of isolated negative vacancies, constant over three decades of concentration. A bath dephases the qubit because its spins exchange spin projections with one another, and two can exchange only if their transition frequencies match. A fine-structure splitting shifts those frequencies. Were every defect on the same crystallographic site, all would shift alike and still match: worth only a factor 1.3. Real defects occupy symmetry-equivalent sites pointing in different directions, so neighbours land at different frequencies and stop exchanging: a further 1.9. What governs the coherence time is therefore the fraction of bath pairs sharing a transition frequency, not the zero-field splitting. Vacancy aggregation extends NV- spin coherence rather than shortening it.

AI.tldr: Contrary to the common assumption that aggregated multi-vacancy complexes dominate decoherence, cluster-correlation-expansion simulations show that a multi-vacancy bath actually extends NV- Hahn-echo coherence times by a factor of 2.7-4.4 compared to isolated negative vacancies at fixed spin density, because symmetry-equivalent sites with differing orientations shift transition frequencies and suppress spin exchange.
AI.motivation: Annealing mobilizes vacancies in semiconductors (Si, SiC, diamond), causing them to aggregate into spin-carrying multi-vacancy complexes. These centers are widely regarded as a magnetic-noise source that degrades spin qubit coherence, and multi-vacancy complexes have been blamed for NV- decoherence in irradiated and implanted diamond. The authors aim to re-examine this attribution and determine the actual role of vacancy aggregation in NV- spin coherence.
AI.method: Cluster-correlation-expansion simulations driven by published electron-paramagnetic-resonance (EPR) parameters were used to model the multi-vacancy bath and compare it with a bath of isolated negative vacancies. The analysis examined how fine-structure splitting and crystallographic site symmetry affect transition-frequency matching among bath spins, thereby controlling spin-projection exchange and dephasing.
AI.result: At a fixed paramagnetic spin density, the multi-vacancy bath yields a Hahn-echo coherence time 2.7-4.4 times longer than a bath of isolated negative vacancies, and this ratio is constant over three decades of concentration. Site-independent fine-structure splitting alone would give only a factor of 1.3, but real defects occupying symmetry-equivalent sites with different orientations produce disparate transition frequencies, adding a further factor of 1.9. The coherence time is governed by the fraction of bath pairs sharing a transition frequency, not by the zero-field splitting.
AI.conclusion: Vacancy aggregation extends rather than shortens NV- spin coherence. The dominant factor is the fraction of bath pairs with matching transition frequencies, which is reduced by the multi-site, multi-orientation nature of real defects, rather than the magnitude of the zero-field splitting.

title: Axial thermal expansion from free-energy minimization with temperature-dependent force constants in phonopy: a technical report, with $α$- and $ω$-Ti as the worked example
summary: In a hexagonal crystal the $a$ and $c$ axes change their lengths at different rates with increasing temperature, and the thermal expansion is described by two coefficients, one for each axis. The equilibrium lattice parameters at each temperature are found by minimizing the Helmholtz free energy over the lattice parameters, and the coefficients are their logarithmic derivatives with respect to temperature. This report describes a procedure for this minimization as implemented in phonopy. The free energy is computed with harmonic force constants at a finite set of values of $a$ and $c$, and a free-energy surface over $a$ and $c$ is fitted to these values. In a variant, the harmonic force constants are replaced by temperature-dependent force constants from a self-consistent harmonic approximation, with the forces computed by a machine-learning potential fitted at each of these values. The $α$ and $ω$ phases of titanium are the worked example. Both calculations give negative thermal expansion of the $c$ axis of $α$-Ti at low temperature and none in $ω$-Ti, and they differ most for the $c$ axis of $α$-Ti. The axial coefficients are harder to compute than the volumetric one, because the two axes are coupled in the free energy. In both phases of titanium the thermal effect that lengthens $a$ also shortens $c$. The coefficient of the $c$ axis is then the sum of two terms of opposite sign that partly cancel, and a small error in either term gives a large relative error in the coefficient. The report measures how much each setting of the procedure changes the thermal expansion coefficients, with the $c$ axis of $α$-Ti as the most sensitive case.

AI.tldr: A procedure in phonopy computes axial thermal expansion coefficients of hexagonal crystals by minimizing the Helmholtz free energy over lattice parameters, using harmonic or self-consistent harmonic force constants. Applied to α- and ω-Ti, it reproduces negative thermal expansion of the c axis in α-Ti and identifies that axis as the most error-sensitive quantity.
AI.motivation: In hexagonal crystals the a and c axes expand at different rates, so two axial coefficients are needed rather than a single volumetric one. Axial coefficients are intrinsically harder to compute because the axes are coupled in the free energy: in both Ti phases the thermal effect that lengthens a also shortens c, so the c-axis coefficient is a sum of two opposing terms that partly cancel, making it highly sensitive to small errors in either term.
AI.method: Equilibrium lattice parameters at each temperature are obtained by minimizing the Helmholtz free energy over a and c, with coefficients taken as logarithmic derivatives with respect to temperature. The free energy is evaluated with harmonic force constants on a finite grid of (a, c) values and a free-energy surface is fitted to them; in a variant, temperature-dependent force constants from a self-consistent harmonic approximation are used, with forces from a machine-learning potential fitted at each grid point. α- and ω-Ti serve as the worked examples.
AI.result: Both calculations yield negative thermal expansion of the c axis of α-Ti at low temperature and none in ω-Ti, with the largest discrepancy between the two approaches for the c axis of α-Ti. The study quantifies how much each setting of the procedure changes the thermal expansion coefficients, identifying the c axis of α-Ti as the most sensitive case.
AI.conclusion: The minimization procedure implemented in phonopy provides axial thermal expansion coefficients for hexagonal crystals, and the comparison of harmonic and self-consistent harmonic treatments shows that the c axis of α-Ti is the most error-sensitive quantity, owing to the partial cancellation of two oppositely signed contributions.

title: On the dual character of Zn impurity in SnTe: Tuning thermoelectric and topological properties
comment: 21 pages + Supplemental Material. Accepted for publication in Physical Review B
summary: We present a first-principles study of the electronic structure and thermoelectric properties of Zn-doped SnTe using the Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker method within the coherent potential approximation, complemented by pseudopotential calculations. SnTe is a lead-free analogue of PbTe and a candidate thermoelectric material in which Zn doping has been experimentally reported to enhance the performance of $p$-type samples. We show that Zn introduces a resonant-like impurity state, located within the conduction band, which evolves strongly depending on the Zn concentration. This feature leads to a significant enhancement of the thermopower in $n$-type SnTe. In the valence band, Zn doping induces L-$Σ$ band convergence, also resulting in an increased $p$-type Seebeck coefficient over a broad concentration range and delaying the onset of the bipolar effect. We further demonstrate that the Zn-induced band-structure modifications drive a transition from an inverted to a trivial band ordering, indicating a controllable topological phase transition. Our results clarify the microscopic role of Zn in SnTe and identify doping as a mechanism for simultaneously tuning thermoelectric and topological properties.

AI.tldr: First-principles study shows Zn doping in SnTe creates a conduction-band resonant impurity state and induces L-Σ valence band convergence, boosting both n- and p-type thermopower and driving a topological phase transition.
AI.motivation: SnTe is a lead-free analogue of PbTe and a promising thermoelectric material. Experiments report that Zn doping enhances p-type performance, but the microscopic origin of this improvement and its broader impact on the electronic structure remain unclear.
AI.method: The electronic structure and thermoelectric properties of Zn-doped SnTe were studied from first principles using the Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker method within the coherent potential approximation (KKR-CPA), complemented by pseudopotential calculations.
AI.result: Zn introduces a resonant-like impurity state inside the conduction band whose character evolves strongly with Zn concentration, greatly enhancing n-type thermopower. In the valence band, Zn doping induces L-Σ band convergence, raising the p-type Seebeck coefficient over a broad concentration range and delaying the bipolar effect. The band-structure changes also drive a transition from inverted to trivial band ordering.
AI.conclusion: Zn's microscopic role in SnTe is clarified, identifying doping as a means to simultaneously tune thermoelectric performance and topological properties, and revealing a controllable topological phase transition.

title: Scandium diboride: a semi-metallic, lattice, thermally matched substrate for vertical AlGaN power electronics
summary: We report the properties of hexagonal (space group P6/mmm) scandium diboride ($\mathrm{ScB}_2$) single crystals grown by a laser diode floating zone method at growth rates of ~1mm/hr under B-rich conditions with (002) rocking curve widths $Δω$=38'' approaching the quality of commercial SiC/GaN substrates. Lattice expansion measurements reveal matching to $\mathrm{Al_{0.55}Ga_{0.45}N}$ with a coefficient of thermal expansion ~5ppm/K at typical AlGaN growth temperatures, enabling thick AlGaN layers for ultra-wide bandgap (UWBG) power electronics >1kV. We measure semi-metallic room temperature resistivity ~15$μΩ$ cm, climbing to ~93$μΩ$ cm at 773K with a $T^2$ dependence effectively eliminating substrate parasitic resistance, the limiting factor in exploiting the full potential of UWBG. The Debye temperature $θ_{D,ScB_2}$ from heat capacity and lattice expansion is ~850K well matched to $θ_{D,ScB_2}$, but lower than the 1100K measured for Sc-rich growth conditions. We discuss Debye matching as a key substrate codesign criterion providing significant overlap in phonon modes for heat removal and thermal matching during AlGaN growth. The competitive thermal conductivity at room temperature 53W/mK is half that from full first principles calculations, a discrepancy we attribute to the presence of Sc-vacancies generated by B-rich growth. while the resistivity is ~2x the theoretical value, indicating that both electrons and phonons play equal role in thermal transport. The smooth ~2.5nm rms roughness surface enables advanced heat removal modalities through engineered phonon bridges and phonon polaritons in $\mathrm{ScB}_2$/AlGaN interfacial heterostructures, potentially allowing ~10-100x increase in power handling over state-of-the-art GaN/SiC.

AI.tldr: High-quality ScB2 single crystals (P6/mmm) are grown by laser diode floating zone, showing lattice/thermal matching to AlGaN, semi-metallic low resistivity with T^2 dependence, and competitive thermal conductivity, positioning ScB2 as a promising substrate for ultra-wide bandgap power electronics.
AI.motivation: Ultra-wide bandgap (UWBG) power electronics such as AlGaN require substrates that enable thick epitaxial layers and efficient heat removal; substrate parasitic resistance and thermal mismatch are limiting factors that motivate the search for better matched, low-loss substrate materials.
AI.method: ScB2 single crystals were grown by a laser diode floating zone method at ~1 mm/hr under B-rich conditions. Structural quality was assessed via (002) rocking curve widths, lattice expansion and coefficient of thermal expansion measurements, resistivity vs. temperature, heat capacity and Debye temperature determination, thermal conductivity measurement, surface roughness characterization, and comparison with first-principles calculations.
AI.result: Crystals show Δω=38'' approaching commercial SiC/GaN quality; lattice matching to Al0.55Ga0.45N with CTE ~5 ppm/K; semimetallic resistivity ~15 μΩ cm at room temperature rising to ~93 μΩ cm at 773K with T^2 dependence; Debye temperature ~850K (lower than 1100K for Sc-rich growth); room-temperature thermal conductivity 53 W/mK, half the first-principles value, attributed to Sc vacancies from B-rich growth, with resistivity ~2x theoretical, indicating equal electron and phonon roles in thermal transport; surface roughness ~2.5 nm rms.
AI.conclusion: ScB2 is a strong substrate candidate for AlGaN-based UWBG power electronics, with Debye matching as a key substrate codesign criterion for phonon overlap and thermal management. Smooth surfaces enable engineered phonon bridges and phonon polaritons at ScB2/AlGaN interfaces, potentially yielding ~10-100x higher power handling than state-of-the-art GaN/SiC.

title: Face-to-face anneal temperature controls lattice parameter in Ta(C,N) virtual substrates for AlGaN power electronics
summary: Tantalum carbide (TaC) thin film ''virtual'' substrates are a highly desirable material for $\text{Al}_{0.5}\text{Ga}_{0.5}\text{N}$ vertical power electronics devices due to lattice matching, thermal expansion matching, and metallic conductivity. However, the material has not been demonstrated to support $\text{Al}_{x}\text{Ga}_{1-x}\text{N}$ layers of variable composition $x$, limiting the range of device applications. We present a method to achieve tunable rock salt $\text{Ta}\text{C}_{x}\text{N}_{1-x}$ virtual substrates via a face-to-face annealing of TaC thin films in an $\text{N}_2$ atmosphere. The results suggest that annealing temperatures below $1600\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ promote partial uptake of nitrogen onto carbon and anion vacancy sites to form rock salt $\text{Ta(C,N)}$ with intermediate anion compositions. At temperatures $\ge 1600\,^{\circ}\text{C}$, nitrogen primarily occupies the anion sublattice and the crystalline quality and surface morphology simultaneously degrade coincident with the formation of secondary phases. This study demonstrates the growth and processing parameters necessary to make tunable lattice constant virtual substrates for $\text{Al}_{x}\text{Ga}_{1-x}\text{N}$ from $x = 0.5\text{-}1$, enabling vertically conducting power electronic devices with reduced defect density at high Al-content.

AI.tldr: Face-to-face annealing of TaC thin films in N₂ enables tunable rock salt TaxCxN1-x virtual substrates, where annealing below 1600 °C gives intermediate anion compositions and ≥1600 °C degrades quality, enabling AlxGa1-xN growth for x = 0.5–1.
AI.motivation: TaC thin film virtual substrates are attractive for Al0.5Ga0.5N vertical power electronics due to lattice matching, thermal expansion matching, and metallic conductivity, but they had not been shown to support AlxGa1-xN layers of variable composition x, restricting device applicability.
AI.method: Face-to-face annealing of TaC thin films in an N2 atmosphere to form rock salt TaxCxN1-x virtual substrates, with varying annealing temperature and characterization of nitrogen uptake, anion composition, crystalline quality, and surface morphology.
AI.result: Annealing below 1600 °C promotes partial nitrogen uptake onto carbon and anion vacancy sites, forming rock salt Ta(C,N) with intermediate anion compositions. At ≥1600 °C, nitrogen primarily occupies the anion sublattice while crystalline quality and surface morphology degrade simultaneously with secondary phase formation.
AI.conclusion: The growth and processing parameters necessary to produce tunable lattice constant virtual substrates for AlxGa1-xN from x = 0.5–1 are established, enabling vertically conducting power electronic devices with reduced defect density at high Al-content.
